[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

‘Words’, Freud said in 1905, ‘are the essential tool of mental treatment’, and these words are written with such conviction that it is perhaps appropriate that Ann Scott reminds us in her Introduction to this year's BJP lecture ‘how hard it can be to translate experience, the reality of the psyche, into language’ (quoting from the editors' Introduction to Mind Readings). Indeed, as this volume will show, the translation of the reality of the psyche is not a straightforward matter of finding the right word. ‘Ideas and experiences that are temporally or intellectually complex often can be understood more clearly from diagrams or maps than from verbal descriptions’ writes Susan Hiller.

Blake Morrison, in his BJP lecture ‘On Childhood and Violence’ painfully reminds us that words, encoded in the form of reports and rules of justice, can be overwhelmed when we are faced with cruelty, brutality and murder. He was a reporter at the trial of Robert Thompson and Jon Venables for the killing of James Bulger and was shocked to discover that right from the beginning the trial violated the 1989 UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. These children were not treated ‘in a manner consistent with the promotion of the child's dignity and worth’. In William Blake's poem, ‘The Clod and the Pebble’ Morrison reminded us that there are:

classic conflicting views we have about children; on the one hand, that they are already, when born, hard little pebbles, intractably themselves, their personalities programmed on some fixed, unalterable course; on the other hand, that they are clods of clay, to be shaped by those around them, so that if we handle them with love and care they will turn out best porcelain, but if we neglect and are careless with them they will break and become ugly.

This is an eloquent image of the eternal debate about how to understand why we do what we do. His lecture was a powerful testimony to the way in which we can become pebble-like at the moment when we need to be more clod-like. Anne Alvarez's response helped us to see more clearly how our failure to love in the face of unspeakable horror is both to be expected and accepted. We need time to be able to get to a state where we can love and forgive. A transcript of the questions and the discussion is given.

Duncan Cartwright

Duncan Cartwright

8 Elland Road, Manor Gardens, Durban 4001, South Africa. email: duncanc@pixie.udw.ac.za

Duncan Cartwright  

The author explores some of the theoretical and clinical problems that the therapist is faced with when dealing with pathological projective identifications. Focusing on the patient's receptive capacity, it is argued that the successful containment of projective identifications, whilst an important part of the therapeutic process, does not adequately account for the patient's capacity to be receptive to realizations pertaining to split off parts of the self. To understand this further, the author makes a conceptual distinction between two inseparable components of the mechanism of projective identification: the affective component and self/object component. It is suggested that the affective component gives rise to problems of receptivity characterized by resistance, whereas the self/object component leads to more difficult problems of incapacity and deficit. The implications this has for therapeutic technique are discussed with particular emphasis placed on the nature, and analysis, of interactive experience as a means of altering the patient's receptivity to previously ‘unthinkable’ parts of the self.

Commentary from a Jungian Perspective

Jean Thomson

Jean Thomson

1 Beatty Street, London, NW1 7IN

Jean Thomson  

My first reaction on reading the case study was to ponder on the patient's permitting the material to be published. The pros and cons went through my mind. The patient must have realized that it is helpful for her therapist's colleagues to have the insights into someone's story. Was this her way of being grateful? Was it reparative? Seeing it all in writing, as I assume she would do, might crystallize something for her and remind her of how she had changed. More negatively, I wondered how much the allowing of herself to be written about was part of the difficulty in retaining and digesting, and how much she felt she would get rid of by having it put on paper and handed to others to read. The case study in other words seemed to me to form, inevitably, part of the therapy process which would in some way be altered by it, and the therapist-writer's work is likely to be influenced in some way, too, by my comments and those of the other commentators.

As a Jungian analyst, I thought, reading the case study, how much I felt at home with it. I thought that the training programmes we go through as psychotherapists are similar and the language we end up with is mostly interchangeable. Most of us, certainly those who style themselves psychoanalytical psychotherapists, and some Jungians do, share an emphasis on work in the transference, keeping in mind the early experiences of the patient. Yet, two factors struck me as different enough, from a Jungian viewpoint, to have a considerable effect on how the material could be understood. Firstly, what the ‘bulimia’ symbolized for the patient and, secondly, the patient's struggle with her ‘femininity’. With the Jungian concept of an original Self, the psyche/soma as an entity from conception, therefore already a being to be realized, becoming as conscious as possible through life experiences, B can be seen to be attempting, through psychotherapy, to follow a need to develop, a need to find some way to learn how to digest experience.

Peter Shoenberg  

Despite extensive developments in the field of psychosomatic medicine, internists, surgeons, gynaecologists, paediatricians, and general practitioners who attend psychosomatic meetings and who take part in colloquia or demonstrations of interviews and psychotherapy have been rarae avaes.

(Maurice Dongier 1977)

Here is a book on the psychotherapy of psychosomatic disorders by one such rare bird. Dr Broom is the founder and director of the Arahura Centre in Christchurch, New Zealand. This medical centre for patients with allergic disorders offers medical and psychotherapeutic assessments and, where appropriate, a brief psychodynamic psychotherapy (i.e. where psychological factors are relevant to the aetiology of the condition). His team comprises general practitioners and psychotherapists. Dr Broom trained initially as a physician and was for some years a researcher in immunology before training as a liaison-consultation psychiatrist and also as a psychotherapist.

His book describes his and his colleagues' medical and psychotherapeutic experiences with these patients. We know from various studies quoted in this book how commonly the somatoform disorders occur in general practice and in hospital settings alike. The figures he quotes suggest that as many as 30 per cent of all attenders in general medical clinics in hospital suffer with somatoform disorders. Also, we know how often in the hospital setting these disorders are either ignored or else managed by non-psychodynamically-oriented liaison-consultation psychiatric services. By a somatoform disorder we usually mean those conditions in which the patient's physical symptoms are produced by a disturbance in bodily function, without any alteration of bodily structure where psychological factors are likely to be causative. These disorders include conversion hysterical reactions, psychogenic pain, body dysmorphic disorder, hypochondriasis and a more complex group of polysymptomatic disorders in which disturbances of body function can lead to the irritable bowel syndrome, chronic fatigue syndrome and neuromuscular tension states. Dr Broom feels that this DSM-IV diagnostic entity is too restrictive and he would like to include those other psychosomatic conditions in which there are additional structural changes to the body, such as bronchial asthma, eczema and ulcerative colitis. This allows him to refer to all these conditions as ‘somatizing’ disorders. Perhaps there is a disadvantage in his less restrictive view in that this view might imply that similar psychopathological mental mechanisms can be attributed to these two rather different groups of psychosomatic disturbance.

Commentary by Two Therapists from the Women's Therapy Centre

Sue Einhorn and Sheila Ritchie

Sheila Ritchie

10 Manor Gardens, London N7 6JS

Sheila Ritchie  

It was very interesting looking at a vignette of clinical work in some detail but also difficult to comment on another therapist's work. Our ideas come from our experience of working with bulimic women at the Women's Therapy Centre, a very different environment from work in private practice although many of the clinical issues are similar.

112

Our first thoughts on discussing the work with this client was the wealth of material produced showing an extremely interesting relationship between therapist and client. We wondered if the therapist, through the process of writing, had absorbed aspects of the client's relationship with her mother. One of us had an immediate countertransference feeling in response to the material and felt that the therapist had already done a lot of the work in a self-sufficient way perhaps in her need to protect the relationship with B. She was almost keeping the reader out as the client had her mother when she shut the bedroom door to protect her privacy.

A further striking aspect to the work was the client's capacity for symbolization emerging through the dreams and fantasies, all of which seemed to resonate with the therapy relationship. This can be unusual with someone who is bulimic where thinking is often more concrete, finding its expression through the language of the body (fat or thin) or the eating itself. It would seem that these dreams and fantasies were the safest way for B to take in the therapy relationship without having to transform it into something that had to be ‘chucked out’.

While the therapist's focus seemed to be on the need for B to mourn her parents' deaths, it did seem to us that what mattered to B was the quality of attention and thinking that the therapist was offering. Perhaps the actual interpretations mattered less than the projected concern that the therapist held for her client. This puts us in mind of Mitchell when he uses Winnicott's material on transitional phenomena:

Personality and growth are created in the potential space between the infant and mother, between any two people in intimate relationships, between analyst and patient. Whose creation personality is can never be determined. It belongs to both the individual and the pair in the relationship'. (Mitchell quoted in Object Relations Theory and Practice: An Introduction by David E. Scharff, 1996)

Shelley MacDonald , Chris Newrith , Fiona Blyth and Gary Winship

Gary Winship

5355 Argyle Rd, Reading RG1 7YL

Gary Winship  

A brief history of ‘rave’ culture is presented. The creation of an ecstatic drug or dance induced euphoria is considered in terms of Freud's (1930) idea that drug intoxication is an inducement of a feeling of ‘oceanic oneness’. It is argued that there is tension in rave culture between pathological narcissism manifest in social withdrawal and the more normalizing process of an adolescent transitional phenomenon in the working through of self/peer identification and deidentification from parents. A key witness account from a semi-structured interview with a male rayer is contextualized with other accounts of rave drawing from popular culture. Based on the ideas of Herbert Rosenfeld, the authors propose a distinction between benign narcissism and its destructive counterpart, malignant narcissism. The context of rave as a subculture of narcissism is considered in terms of government leadership during the 1980s and the ‘trickle up trickle down’ effect of social stratum reciprocity (Habermas 1989).

[[RunningHead]]

Is it Still Possible to Publish?

Chris Maloney

Chris Maloney

Ascot, Berks

Chris Maloney  

Dear Editor

Jane Polden's article ‘Publish and Be Damned’ (British Journal of Psychotherapy 14(3): 337-347) addresses an increasingly thorny problem in the healthcare field, and one that is particularly difficult for psychotherapists. The details omitted from physical medicine's case reports to guarantee a patient's anonymity are the very details of concern to the psychotherapist - the patient's unique personality. This echoes the philosophical difficulties in applying statistical methods to psychotherapeutic work, wherein a method that takes what is unique to every individual and disregards it is used to study a practice that selectively focuses on the very thing that is being disregarded.

Polden considers the dynamics of the current way of writing up case material for publication. The conclusion that one inevitably draws is that it is impossible. Many of the objections may be overcome by asking patients for consent, but this path is itself fraught with problems. When do you consult the patient? Anyone who has written a clinical paper knows that its conception is not easy, and a great deal of labour goes into producing it. Consent must then surely be obtained at the conception phase: but is the patient consulted again - and do they ultimately have a right of veto at the end? Indeed, should the model be one of (perhaps repeated) permission, or is there an alternative?

There may be greater scope for collaborative production of papers (such as with Mary Barnes and Joe Berke), where the patient is a co-creator of the narrative, and contributor to the theoretical points that are made. This collaboration might challenge the ‘paternalistic’ model, which seems implicit in Polden's article (since it reflects current practice), where it is the therapist alone who does the writing and determines the content. Methodologically, however, a change to a dyadic method could open up a new way of producing rigorous analytic theory, at the same time as elegantly solving many ethical problems around publication. Psychoanalytic theory would cease to be ‘a closed system’ in the way it has been to date.

Dr Horowitz's case presents us with what must be the ultimate problem in psychoanalytic treatment - the analysand who does not talk and does not come to his sessions. Dr Horowitz struggles courageously with these difficulties. As the narrative ends the treatment seems to have taken hold. The patient is able to resume a medical

career interrupted long ago. He experiences an improved working alliance with his analyst and enhanced empathy for others. Dr Horowitz conceptualizes these improvements as occurring through the interpretation of the mutually constructed analytic relationship.

As a self psychologist, my way of accounting for the changes in the patient is somewhat different from Dr Horowitz's. Mr L presented in a fragmenting state. The course of the treatment led to the reconstitution of a positive paternal selfobject transference which had merger and idealizing elements. Mr L's initial state of devitalization was also converted to a condition of incompletely modulated grandiosity. I would expect this primitive form of grandiosity to continue to be modified and integrated in an increasingly realistic fashion as the treatment progresses. In short, a healthy growth process involving analyst and patient has replaced a pathologically stunted one. One might say that Mr L is having a ‘corrective emotional experience’.

Initially, the demands of treatment were almost too much for Mr L. The analyst's neutrality felt so much like his father's neglect that Mr L could barely speak, or even come to his sessions. To Mr L, temporary withdrawal must have seemed the only way he could regulate the repetition of his childhood trauma. Yet there was hope, based on the fact that Mr L had been able to form a usable positive transference to Dr P in the past. I suspect that Mr L must have perceived that Dr Horowitz was trying very hard on his behalf. This preconscious awareness saved the day and enabled them both to survive the rage, paranoia and re-enactment of abuse and abandonment of the early stages of the analysis.

Female member of the audience: I've done a certain amount of work with young delinquents, and I think in children of this type that you have been lecturing about, you feel that there is an enormous identification between the aggressor and the victim. It's as though there is an internalized aggressor and victim in the child. The assault on the victim is a way of externalizing the inner victim in the aggressor. It's as though the only alternative to being a victim is to be the aggressor. Just as if you were perhaps treating the victim in more favourable circumstances, you might try to liberate this aggression because, for them, the only alternative to being a victim is to be an aggressor. You notice in groups where a child is being bullied, where a group of children are all bullying one child, that they all seem to be saying: ‘He is the victim, not me’. They choose a vulnerable child so that they can externalize their own victim, get rid of it, on that child.

Blake Morrison: It may be worth pointing out that Jon Venables had actually had to move schools because he was being bullied, and had had a period off school, and that Robert was thought by his own family to be rather gentle - I mean, he had a habit of sucking his thumb and he was thought of as the gentle one among the Thompson boys.

Ann Scott: If I could make a comment. It occurs to me that one of the points that you [Blake Morrison] are making implies that an individual would have a sense of what it would be to be a victim. David Smith is right to emphasize that I state that Ferenczi never appealed to the veracity of patients' testimony. He is also correct in his assumption that I equally reject the claim that Ferenczi believed in the veracity of patients' perceptions of their analysts, a claim he contrasts with my ‘transference paradigm which describes patients' perceptions of analysts as fundamentally distorted’ (Smith 1998, p. 348). In this context, he suggests that to ‘neutralize’ this claim, I need to demonstrate that Myers (1996) has systematically misconstrued Ferenczi, and he challenges me specifically to provide an alternative reading of the following passage, which he quotes as follows:

Gradually, then, I came to the conviction that the patients have an exceedingly refined sensitivity for the wishes, tendencies, whims, sympathies and antipathies of their analyst, even if the analyst is completely unaware of this sensitivity… This means that we must discern not only the painful events from their associations, but also - and much more often than hitherto supposed - their repressed or suppressed criticism of us. (Ferenczi [1933a]1955, pp. 157-158, cited in Myers 1996, p. 28)

First of all, the term ‘veracity’ (Wahrhaftigkeit) does not figure in this passage, which is taken from Ferenczi's (1933) ‘Confusion of tongues’ paper, nor in the Clinical Diary (1988), which Myers and Smith take as their principal source, and it appears very rarely indeed in Ferenczi's work as a whole. When it is mentioned, it is mentioned problematically in the context of verification (Wahrheitsnachweis) of analytical explanations. In ‘Transitory symptom-constructions during the analysis’ (Ferenczi 1912), for example, Ferenczi states that:

So long as the psychical material afforded through free association is the only proof that the patient has of the correctness of the analytical explanations, they may seem to him remarkable, surprising, even illuminating; he still does not attain a conviction of their indubitable correctness, the feeling that they are the only explanations possible, however honestly he may try to become convinced, or even if he forces conviction on himself with all his strength. It definitely looks as if one could never reach any real convictions at all through logical insight alone; one needs to have lived through an effective experience, to have - so to speak - felt it on one's own body, in order to gain that degree of certain insight which deserves the name of ‘conviction’ (Gewissheit). (Ferenczi [1912]1952, pp. 193-194)

An Attachment-Based Approach to Working with Clients Affected by HIV and AIDS: A Reply to Jill Brown's Response

Chris Purnell

Chris Purnell

5 St Lukes Road, Doseley, Telford, Shropshire TF4 3BE

Chris Purnell  

I noted with interest Jill Brown's (1997) response to my paper ‘An attachment-based approach to working with clients affected by HIV and AIDS’ (Purnell 1996). There are a number of points which she raises to which I feel it would be helpful to respond.

I do agree with Brown that the paper which I presented made psychotherapy with HIV-affected clients ‘sound like extremely hard work’. It can be, but to suggest that this work was ‘driven by anxiety and, possibly, a need to counter the negative transference’ is plainly inaccurate. What it reflects is the complexity of issues - biological, psychological and social - which need to be addressed when working with this particular client group. It is not collective anxiety which has led to the development of the ‘new model of counselling’ which she questions the need for, but a recognition that old paradigms do not adequately meet the challenge which HIV and AIDS present.

Perhaps this is also where some of Brown's difficulty with what I am saying lies. The attachment model which I present does not fit neatly into older and more established paradigms. There is no reason why it should, and the fact that it doesn't does not make it any less valid - there is a rich and exciting body of attachment research which continues to grow out of Bowlby's original formulations, and which becomes increasingly difficult to ignore. The temptation is to try and assimilate this into more traditional paradigms rather than develop something new, drawing only, where appropriate, upon psychoanalytic theory.

It may be, as Brown quotes, that practitioners who work within a psychoanalytic framework ‘do not need to alter that framework unduly for these patients’, but what also needs to be recognized is that some clients who are living with HIV do not readily find the traditional psychoanalytic framework conducive to their needs for psychological support.

Very often for those affected the difficulties lie not simply within their own internal processes in dealing with loss, illness, death and dying, but also within an external environment which is riddled with hostile attitudes to those who are affected by HIV. The point which I am attempting to make in my paper is that clients can put a lot of energy into coping with living with the virus, and may have the inner resources do so quite successfully. They may not perceive a need for counselling, however, they are still having to deal with loss and can benefit from a relationship which can help them to do this.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

After the recent tidal wave of criticism of Freud and psychoanalysis, we are left on the shores to calculate the damage. Some of psychoanalysis's most vociferous critics would like to believe that it was a cultural hallucination that Freud's body of theory was ever important in the first place. Listed among his many errors is the charge that Freud borrowed and stole from other traditions, from hypnosis as I heard in a recent paper, plundering its literature and claiming it as his own. But this is a narrow reading of Freud - his thinking lies much more in the legacy of the rational system-builders of the Philosophy of Mind in the early nineteenth century, Kant and Hegel, and will stand with these. Before Freud's systematic model of the mind appeared, little was done to help those with mental disturbance and distortions of thinking. Freud's humanizing effect is sometimes forgotten, that a disturbed person can be carefully listened to with attention and understanding over a long period, and be changed thereby. In these less humane and patient times, we rebuild on the shores.

More than an aetiological explanation, psychoanalysis is, above all, a technique. How we spend our time with patients, how we do it, is of the greatest interest in our evolving profession. The BJP is keen to have more papers on clinical work, the ordinary workaday sessions and the way in which we talk to patients when we interpret defences, transference, dreams, etc. Although we give priority to articles that make an original contribution, a new idea placed within the literature and argued cogently with case examples, we also need more accounts of our everyday work for the purposes of thinking and discussion. I hope readers will respond.

The two great sources of energy and motivation, love and aggression, find their place in this issue. Firstly, Hester Solomon writes of the many forms of love in analytic work, stressing love of the mother for her infant in the first months as formative for mental growth, bringing in the new research by Allan Schore. Then, Richard Tillett writes of therapist difficulties in the face of aggressive feelings toward patients. This is a highly controversial area in view of our counsel of containment and non-retaliation as basic to the analytic stance. Tillett argues that countertransference hate and aggression can be used effectively for therapeutic gains, moving the therapy forward, modelling a safe use of aggression and thereby deepening the relationship.

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Stevenage

Phil Mollon  

This is a timely collection of 13 papers relating to the controversies about recovered and false memory. These cover clinical, theoretical and legal issues. The general orientation is psychoanalytic.

Prozan, the editor, is a feminist psychoanalyst who has herself been a prey in the hunting of therapists by those who propagate the concept of false memory syndrome. Her account, reproduced here, of the reconstruction of early sexual abuse in the background of her patient, Penelope, has been fiercely attacked by Freud-bashers such as Ofshe, a sociologist, and Crews, a professor of literature. More psychoanalytically sophisticated commentaries upon the case of Penelope are provided here by Stephen Seligman and Katherine MacVicar.

Seligman highlights the political dimension inherent in Prozan's position:

… If the clinical situation always contains a political background, the treatment of women who were molested by trusted men during their childhood brings the sexual-political questions toward the foreground. As is often true when issues become politicized and especially when secrecy is at issue, it is impossible to avoid taking a stand…. For her [Prozan], analysis, feminism, and critical social thinking are synergistic rather than inconsistent. (p. 216)

In ‘Psychic reality and historical truth’, Howard Levine describes the evolution of Freud's theorizing on memory and its clinical implications. He presents some apt quotes from Freud which would not be out of place today as informed observations on the unreliability of memory as a record of literal truth. Levine emphasizes that there is nothing inherent in the affective quality or presentation of an apparent memory which would enable a reliable distinguishing of true from false; moreover, clinical improvement may occur on the basis of an incorrect interpretation or reconstruction. He concludes that the psychotherapist must steer a path between the extremes of excessive scepticism and too-ready belief' (p. 16).

A particularly interesting chapter is provided by Ephraim Margolin, one of the lawyers for Gary Romona who successfully sued his daughter's hospital and therapists for a variety of forms of malpractice - ‘unprofessional agenda-driven treatment’ - which led to her ‘memories’ of his having raped her. Margolin raises a number of interesting and worrying questions about the legal implications: if a counsellor or therapist appears to persuade a client that dissolution of an abusive marriage is desirable, should the children or other relatives have a right to sue the therapist? If questions can play a part in implanting a false memory, how cautious should therapists be in exploring a client's history? How elaborate and explicit should informed consent for therapy be?

Snoo Wilson

Snoo Wilson

Snoo Wilson  

In the roaring twenties, right in the downward swing of the Jazz Age, an impetuous, only partly educated American 20 something-year-old embarked on a series of ‘active imagination’ trances in Zurich, Switzerland. Married, she had previously had a fling with Chaim Weizmann. The founder of Israel had already had quite a turnover of good-looking American girls. But she was clearly special.

Claire Douglas's meticulous and well-sourced study engagingly traces the life and times as well as the ancestry of a quite remarkable woman whose history till now has been obscured; akin to an unknown rock, concealed beneath the rusty waters under the ramshackle seaside pier of Jungian analysis.

With Jung's encouragement, Christiana produced a welter of spirited primal adventures, consumed by snakes, coupling with giant negroes, and providing Jung with a massive store of fantasy data. Like Freud, he was able to behave like a boutique shopper selecting whatever suited his own interpretation of that obscure and still contentious domain, the unconscious. Later, she protested at the way he had used the material, but seems to have forgiven him when he visited the Harvard Psychological Clinic in the thirties.

Modes of Therapeutic Action

Enrico E. Jones

The dialectic in psychoanalysis between theories about the mutative effects of interpretation and psychological knowledge and those concerning the effects of interpersonal interaction constitutes an important tension for approaches to psychoanalytic technique. This essay briefly summarizes the thinking around these alternative conceptualizations of therapeutic action, and introduces a new empirically derived model, that of ‘repetitive interaction structure’, which attempts to bridge therapeutic action by insight and by relationship. Interaction structure is a way of formulating those aspects of the analytic process that have come to be termed intersubjectivity, transference-countertransference enactments and role responsiveness. The concept operationalizes important aspects of interpersonal interaction, and can help specify the two-person patterns that emerge in an analysis. Patient and analyst interact in repetitive ways; these patterns of interaction, which are slow to change, probably reflect the psychological structure of both patient and analyst, whether psychic structure is conceptualized in terms of object-representations or compromise formations and impulse-defence configurations. Therapeutic action is located in the experience, recognition and understanding by patient and analyst of these repetitive interactions. Interaction structures stress the importance of the intrapsychic as a basis for what becomes manifest in the interactive field Clinical illustrations from a psychoanalysis are provided, and research on repetitive interaction structures is described.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis78, 1119, 1997

A Matrix of Hysteria

Nitza Yarom

The psychoanalytic literature of the last decades on hysteria is reviewed and its overemphasis on pre-oedipal concepts is demonstrated. A matrix of hysteria, which is a contemporary rereading of Freud's basic conceptualization, is presented. It integrates oedipal concepts with others borrowed from object-relations theories, self-psychology and the intersubjective approach. In this way the focus on the issues of gender and sexuality in hysteria is continued, without the original roots being lost. The focus is on the content, and the structure may vary. Within the first axis of the matrix, the author proposes to identify the conflict of gender and sexual identity as the unconscious and conscious solutions that a hysteric adopts to the question ‘am I a man or a woman?’ In an attempt to identify hysteria's particular psychic dynamics, a range of concepts is suggested. Repression and conversion are incorporated to constitute the second and third axes of the matrix. Repression, denial, dissociation and fantasy are shown to be employed in the context of gender and sexuality and along a continuum of personality structures. In this context, the turning to the body, the conversion, still acts as an effective language, to which we have to listen.

This is above all a courageous book. For most people - and that includes most therapists - ageing is a phenomenon or process which, if they think about it at all, they look at from the outside. Ageing is what happens to other people. It is not the count of years that matters: most of us can deal easily enough, both in our professional and our nonprofessional relations, with people noticeably older (or indeed younger) than we are. But part of our ease in doing so comes from the comforting assumption that we ourselves are free of these noticeable markings. Maybe nobody would call us young, but then nobody would call us old either. In fact, we're just about right: we're well past the anxieties of the young, and haven't yet run into the fears of the old. Many readers of this journal will work for some of their time in the public sector, either in the National Health Service itself, as I do, or, as the editor of this book, in other public institutions such as universities. This book explores both the changes in political philosophy which have led a new culture of management of the public health services, and the consequent experiences of those who have to engage with this, and the demands this makes.

When I left an earlier career in educational administration I undertook to myself that, in my new career, I would keep away from managing and management and concentrate on the clinical. I am not sure whether I believed it at the time, but I have not kept to it.

I meet regularly with a number of colleagues who, like me, work as counsellors in GP practices in South London, and one continuing strand within our group is anxiety at whether the local Health Commission will continue to fund us and the work we do. For those of us who work within fund holding practices there is a further anxiety about whether the practice will decide to retain us. One person has recently lost her job because, it seems, the practice ceased to appreciate her work within their framework of values where effectiveness is measured within a narrow notion of cost, which is confined to the cost of treatment, and which excludes the wider costs, financial and otherwise, of not treating the patient.

One of our continuing tasks is to find a way, or ways, of demonstrating what we believe is our effectiveness, when it is hard to establish criteria of this which are valid for us, and which will be convincing to those whom we need to convince, whose value systems are quite different.

It is tempting not to continue this struggle, to close the consulting-room door and concentrate on the clinical. It is difficult that we feel that the boundary of our work is not sufficiently held by others so that we have to struggle to hold it ourselves, when a vital part of our clinical work is holding this boundary for our patients. In Winnicottian terms we have to be both the mother and the father.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis78, 877, 1997

The Elusive Concept of ‘Internal Objects’ (1934-1943): Its Role in the Formation of the Klein Group

R. D. Hinshelwood

The author traces a debate about the concept of ‘internal objects’ that took place between 1937 and 1943 at a time when a group of British analysts was forming around Melanie Klein. The debate is set within a complex of personal, group and organizational dynamics, which the paper makes a start on unravelling The history of the British Psycho-Analytical Society at this time exemplifies Bion's notion of group schism. The events in the Society's history demonstrate defensive aspects of the interaction between the opposed groups, which support members against various anxieties. These include the stress of the work of analysis, but also in this instance the particular anxieties deriving from the collapse of psychoanalysis in Europe, the state of war of the country as a whole, and the death of Freud shortly after he came to London. This psychoanalytic anxiety/defence model clarifies some aspects of the debate about internal objects, and demonstrates the way in which these various anxieties and defences become organized around a scientific debate in a scientific society.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis78, 899, 1997

Personal Experiences - Professional Interests: Joan Riviere and Femininity

M. Athol Hughes

The author proposes that the subject chosen for psychoanalytical investigation bears a relationship to autobiographical experiences. Aspects of the life of the British psychoanalyst, Joan Riviere (1883-1962), are examined and related to her investigation into a form of pathological femininity presented in her paper ‘Womanliness as a masquerade’. Information about her formative years is gained from a diary kept by her mother that gives details of Joan Riviere's early months and years as well as further information about her as a young adult. Riviere's own diary, which lists events and activities in which she took part throughout more than a decade before she became a psychoanalyst, gives valuable insights into her life at that time. The author examines the descriptions of the patient in Riviere's paper and relates it to many facets of the latter's life. The defensive femininity shown by her patient is characterized by appeasement and denial of intellectual and professional attributes to escape detection and the retribution feared as a consequence of having, in phantasy, stolen potency from men. It is suggested that Riviere's own life experiences, particularly in relation to men, are represented in her paper.

This is an important and interesting contribution to the development of our understanding of offender patients. It is number three in a series, Forensic Focus, edited by Murray Cox. This volume offers the experience of psychoanalytic psychotherapists working with a wide range of problems, largely within the NHS. The chapters are individual, though the contributors (all female) were part of a study group run by the editors.

In Part I, the editors in their foreword briefly outline the history and development of forensic psychiatry and psychotherapy, and include a chapter on the assessment of offender patients. Some of the issues raised in management and treatment are developed further in a chapter by Dr C. Taylor.

In Part II contributors discuss a wide range of cases and topics. Presentations are individual and of a high standard. There is liberal use of case vignettes which ‘come alive’ for the reader. Included are incest, violent and non-violent offending, murder, abuse, perversions, fraud and other problematic behaviours, rooted in the bleak and damaged internal worlds of the patients. Certain themes recur: the pain of this sort of work for the patient, the therapist and others; the need for careful understanding of transference and countertransference, and for personal therapy, supervision, and a supportive network. These measures may help mitigate and contain the splits and conflicts driven by, and mirroring, the damaged internal worlds of the patients. The contributors, whilst acknowledging the pain and struggle, manage to convey their ability to hang on to some hope.

Mary Medlicott

Mary Medlicott

Berks

Mary Medlicott  

Therapeutic storymaking or TSM is a short-term method for groups of individuals who have specific need for therapeutic help. Developed, practised and taught by Alida Gersie over a number of years, the method is closely related to dramatherapy and other arts therapies. Suitable for various kinds of client groups ranging from those with mental health problems to frail, elderly people, it draws on the basic belief that we are our stories and that our functioning in the world is closely related to our varying abilities to know and to tell them.

In two previous books, Gersie described the use of stories and storytelling activities in therapy and education and in bereavement counselling. The current work feels like a kind of homecoming. Focusing squarely on the beliefs and techniques of TSM itself and giving numerous short and long descriptions of the method in practice, it clearly sets out the three different kinds of story which Gersie acknowledges as part of the process - the traditional tale represented by myth and folk-tale; the personal autobiographical story; and the fantasy-type story which can be created on the spot by individuals. This analysis in turn facilitates helpful accounts of various ways of working with these three types of story, a clear view of the potential within them and an understanding of how different stories and types of story relate to each other and to people generally. The book also deals well with the system of response tasks which Gersie has created as a technique by which individuals in groups may respond to the stories they hear and, through so doing, address the needs of the individuals who tell them, often, initially, with considerable timidity and fear.

The resulting method has significant differences from group therapy as classically practised. In group therapy, there is no agenda.

This book's purpose is to explore what ‘analysts draw on in order to enter into and elucidate the minds of others’ (p. 1). To this end, Hamilton considers that the analyst's contribution is not fully captured by ideas of countertransference. She resurrects and expands upon Freud's idea of the preconscious, standing as it does between the conscious and unconscious, with other ‘in-between’ concepts, namely Winnicott's and Balint's ideas of the ‘third’ or ‘intermediary’ areas. She particularly sees the preconscious as an area of play and imagination.

With these premises in mind, Hamilton has undertaken an extensive research project using interviews and questionnaires with psychoanalysts in the UK and USA. Altogether she interviewed 65 analysts from a broad spectrum of psychoanalytic perspectives, Kleinians, self psychologists, American eclectics, British Independents, Los Angeles Freudians and others. From the interviews and questionnaires the author then divides her data up into various headings for each chapter, such as the nature of psychic truth, objective reality and the real relationship; holding and containment; the analytic model of change and so forth. Each chapter explores these themes through the expressed opinions of representatives of the various theoretical groups. The book is laid out in such a manner as to allow these contrasting views to be compared.

A book linking child abuse, therapy and the law is long overdue. Kennedy promises in his introduction that what is to follow ‘is based on the assumption that the legal framework can help those working in the mental health field and a psychotherapeutic understanding of groups, families and individuals can aid lawyers in steering families more effectively through the legal process’. Would that this was possible! He is right to point out that the legal process used effectively can be of assistance to mental health professionals and, more importantly, to the children they serve. He also usefully highlights that a psychotherapeutic understanding can be beneficial to lawyers and their clients.

The book is a fascinating account of the Cassel Hospital's work with families, but it fails to deliver in terms of making the legal connections. There remains a book to be written in this area and Roger Kennedy gives enough indicators in this book that he is the person to write it. What is required is the detail of how the links can be made on a case by case basis and some analysis of how the legal process impacts on the abused child and his/her family.

Where Child Abuse, Psychotherapy and the Law does have enormous strength is in the detailed case studies of families treated at the Cassel. The work is described with families with severe emotional and psychological problems that have resulted in the child(ren) being abused. Fascinating links are made between psychoanalytic concepts, family systems theory and ideas regarding the therapeutic community and how these are brought to bear on the assessment and treatment of the families in residence.

The work is essentially child centred, reflecting the 1989 Children Act in which the child's rights are paramount. parents' capacities, as parents, are assessed from a psychoanalytic perspective. Any deficits in parental authority and responsibility are analysed in relation to the ‘child within’ the parent. It is evident that problems in the parents' own childhood have often led to destructive and negative behaviour in adulthood that can be magnified when children are born. This can awaken past conflicts and re-open old wounds. The child can become the object on which the family focuses and which can unite and divide it. Relationships become skewed as the child is given object status. He or she ceases to be perceived as a person but is related to merely as a function.

Chris Maloney

Chris Maloney

Ascot, Berkshire SL5 8AA

Chris Maloney  

Introduction

All psychic phenomena have a personal and a collective component. This paper is an attempt to understand some of the anxieties besetting the profession of psychotherapy in terms of ubiquitous patterns of primate behaviour. It has arisen from the experience of establishing a training in psychotherapy within the UK National Health Service. This is a training in what might be termed psychoanalytical, or psychodynamic, psychotherapy: the issue of which name to use lies at the heart of the paper. The difficulty arose not so much because of internal uncertainty, as because of anxieties about identity apropos the profession as a whole. In the event, we settled the issue of ‘what type of training are we?’ fairly easily, but with some disquiet about the process. This process will be analysed in a way that throws light on the way that names and theory are used within the culture of psychotherapy. On a personal level, the paper is an attempt to exorcize material that has preoccupied me at various times during two years of difficult negotiation and course development. The material is curiously compelling (for reasons that will become clear), but it is ultimately a psychological cul-de-sac.

The Four Counties Training

There has long been recognition of the need for high quality training in psychoanalytically based psychotherapy within the public sector (Richards & Murphy 1995). Since late 1995 a training in Psychodynamic Psychotherapy in Health Service Settings has been developed by an association of NHS Psychotherapy Services in the old Oxford Region, now known as the Four Counties. We provide a Master's programme collaboratively with Oxford Brookes' University, and are affiliated to the UPA, through which we are undergoing accreditation to enable graduates to register with UKCP. The course is well supported by local NHS Trusts, and our first intake will graduate in 2001.

It has been a considerable achievement to get this far. The development has involved coordinating joint action between a number of independent psychotherapy services, to establish a consensus on what each thought a training would be, and to find a way of speaking with a common voice. This was in parallel with selling the idea to managers and Trusts, who would be committing scarce resources.

Transferences and Countertransferences: The Cognitive Analytic Therapy Perspective

Anthony Ryle DM FRCPsych

Anthony Ryle

London SE1 9RT

Anthony Ryle  

Transference-countertransference phenomena are examined from the theoretical viewpoint of Cognitive Analytic Therapy. Patient-therapist relationships are described as one example of a more general model of relationships. The common origins and parallel features of intrapersonal relationships between aspects of the self and interpersonal relationships with others are emphasized. The practical value of describing these features early in therapy, so that the shifting, complex course of the therapy relationship can be precisely recognized, is presented. As part of this, the model proposes a distinction between identifying and reciprocating transference and countertransference patterns. These CAT understandings can be of value in supervision and case management as well as in therapy, and may be of value to therapists working in other modes.

Deep Calling Unto Deep: Artistic Creativity and the Maternal Object

Ken Wright

Ken Wright

Magdalen Road, Hadleigh, Suffolk IP7 5AD

Ken Wright  

Introduction

Transitional phenomena occupy a central place in the thought of Donald Winnicott (Winnicott 1951, 1971), and Winnicott himself sketched a developmental path from such early creations to the larger worlds of culture and religion (Winnicott 1967a, 1971). In the present paper I want to build on this idea and draw out its implications for the creative process.

According to Winnicott, transitional phenomena are constituted in the first year of life when certain ordinary objects become endowed with special significance. Winnicott regarded them as occupying a transitional place in symbolic development. Not yet separate enough to be fully fledged symbols, they are nevertheless more than mere objects, having been endowed by the infant with personal meaning.

Typically, the transitional object is the comforting bit of blanket that the infant mouths and caresses. Winnicott called it the ‘first “not-me” possession’ but he saw it as a very special possession which the infant had in some sense created.

The notion that the baby under certain circumstances might be able to create its objects is central to Winnicott's theory of personal development. Only when the baby is allowed such an experience can the world be endowed with personal meaning; and only then can there be a lively and creative involvement with the world.

It was not Winnicott, but another psychoanalyst, Michael Balint (1959), who coined the phrase ‘harmonious mix-up’ to capture this interpenetration of subject and object in early experience. Balint's term referred to the early relationship with the mother but could equally be applied to the transitional object. Indeed, Winnicott sometimes called such an object a subjective object precisely because of the mix-up of subjective and objective in its constitution. In the bit of blanket, for example, it seemed that the experienced sensory properties of the object - its softness, warmth, and perhaps its smell - somehow embodied an earlier subjective experience with the mother. Like a shrine which the baby had unwittingly made, the bit of blanket preserved within its sensory qualities elements of an earlier experience which the baby still needed.

Ferenczi, Langs and Scientific Reasoning: A Reply to Martin Stanton

David Smith

David Smith

8 Brenchley Gardens, London SE23 3QS. E-mail: 100131.575@compuserve.com

David Smith  

I would like to give a brief response to Martin Stanton's (1997) severely critical comments on Piers Myers's (1996) paper ‘Sandor Ferenczi and patients' perceptions of analysis’.

In his paper, Myers kindly acknowledges me as the first writer to comment on the relationship between some of Ferenczi's ideas during the 1930s and the concepts developed by Robert Langs in the 1970s (Smith 1991). Myers has investigated these matters very deeply, and has extended and corrected errors in my own account. By any standard, Myers's work is an important contribution to the history of ideas in psychoanalysis.

Stanton is anxious to refute two claims made by Myers. The first of these is the claim that, towards the end of his life, Ferenczi was concerned with the veracity of patients' perceptions of their analysts (as opposed to the transference paradigm, which describes patients' perceptions of their analysts as fundamentally distorted). According to Stanton (1997) ‘Ferenczi never appealed to the “veracity” of patients' testimony’ (my italics) (p. 556). In his paper, Myers provides us with evidence taken from Ferenczi's writings which strongly corroborate his claim. In order to neutralize Myers's argument, Stanton would need to demonstrate that Myers has systematically misconstrued Ferenczi. In order to defend his own thesis effectively, and to refute the claims made by Myers (and myself), Stanton needs to supply alternative interpretations of the meaning of passages like the following:

Gradually, then, I came to the conviction that the patients have an exceedingly refined sensitivity for the wishes, tendencies, whims, sympathies and antipathies of their analyst, even if the analyst is completely unaware of this sensitivity… This means that we must discern not only the painful events from their past from their associations, but also - and much more often than hitherto supposed - their repressed or suppressed criticism of us (1933, cited in Myers 1996, p. 28).

I would be grateful if Dr Stanton would provide a cogent argument to show that this and similar passages do not demonstrate Ferenczi's concern with patients' veridical perceptions of their analysts.

Trauma, Memory and Memorials

Michael Rowlands

Michael Rowlands

Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT

Michael Rowlands  

Introduction

In the last two decades we have witnessed a tremendous growth in both the building of war memorials and in writings about them. The memorial sites of the First World War now receive more visitors than ever before; in the last ten years there have been several new competitions for memorials for Holocaust victims and the Vietnam Veterans Memorial on the Washington Mall has become perhaps the most famous and one of the most visited monuments of the late twentieth century. The need to build memorials is also beginning to spread outside the West as can be seen in the monument built to commemorate the war of independence in Zimbabwe and the debate on how to remember the victims of genocide in Cambodia. This, of course, does not inevitably mean a late twentieth century or late capitalist obsession with mass death nor that the experience of traumatic violence inevitably becomes a public act of relief from private misery in public bereavement and mourning but it does suggest that the need to ‘find out’ what happened, that the process of coming to terms is now and probably always has been more complicated than a passive acceptance that ‘they died for a good cause’.

The question I wish to ask is why some monuments ‘work’ at the personal level of healing and reconciliation whilst others evoke distaste and condemnation. The latter is particularly true of the minimalist architecture of some recent memorials which have aroused considerable controversy. Rachel Whiteread's winning composition for the new memorial to the Holocaust victims to be built on the site of a medieval Jewish synagogue in Vienna remains, because of local opposition, a design waiting to be unveiled. James Young explains popular resistance to modernist memorials as due to the inadequacy of these sites to gather together personal memories into a collective space (Young 1993). The implication that the visual structure of a monument fails to encourage certain kinds of remembering and forgetting as part of a healing process raises an interesting point that we may better be able to understand how it works negatively, through what people dislike. However, it is also true that some memorials are successful not by encouraging remembrance but rather by the demands they make for recognition of what was done, to whom and by whom. The expectation for confessions, expiations and reparations is therefore not too distant from these controversies over the aptness of visual form.

Joy Schaverien

Joy Schaverien  

This paper is offered with the aim of alerting practitioners to the implications of the Holocaust in the experiences of Jewish clients who may themselves be unaware of its significance. Many Jewish people who come for psychotherapy today were not necessarily, nor apparently, directly affected by the Holocaust and yet they carry the inter generational scars. Beginning with my own personal experience, as well as the insight I have gained from conducting analytical art psychotherapy groups on Jewish identity, I will show how subtle and pervasive is the legacy of the Holocaust. The paper is based in Jewish experience but there are implications for work with refugees and immigrants from many other current situations. Discussion includes consideration of some of the psychological affects of anti-semitism. The intention is to draw attention to issues which may not be immediately apparent when people first come for analysis or psychotherapy.

Trainees and Clinical Experience

Dear Editor

I couldn't believe my eyes when I read the article by Moli Paul and Gill Bluck (1997). It was in the section entitled ‘Training Experiences in Psychotherapy’, but I didn't find any training in the article. I just found an extraordinary situation where two doctors were thrown into doing ‘psychodynamic’ psychotherapy with no training at all. They did have supervision, and hence some kind of feedback, but even this was not based on their actual performance, but only on their notes. I seriously wonder if the Uffculme Clinic have not gone collectively mad. This is not, repeat not, the way to do training in psychotherapy. If the Clinic had wanted to institute such a practice, they could easily have consulted established training centres within the UKCP or the BCP for advice and assistance. But to ask people to carry out psychodynamic psychotherapy with no personal analysis and no skills training cannot be right. The prospect of seeing doctors ‘progressing into a career in this specialty’ (p. 222) on the basis of non-training like this fills me with horror.

Yours sincerely

John Rowan

London

In Dialogue with Stephen Mitchell

Susie Orbach

Susie Orbach

2 Lancaster Drive, London NW3 4HA

Susie Orbach  

It's customary at such occasions to say what a pleasure or an honour it is to be a respondent. So habitual is this pleasantry that the intended meaning of such words is bleached out, rendering the preliminary remarks simply a mannered nicety which is a prelude to the respondent's remarks. By contrast, I want to emphasize how very authentic is my delight and honour to be able to participate in this event with Stephen Mitchell in this way.

Stephen Mitchell is among two or three of the most significant North American analysts of today. His project, as I have understood it, has several parts to it. At the base of it is a passion for understanding human subjects and what we have learned about ourselves through the discipline of psychoanalysis. One strand has been to superbly explicate psychoanalytical theory and theory about the practice of psychoanalysis - I'm thinking of his first book with Greenberg, Object Relations in Psychoanalytic Theory (1983), and his 1995 book, Freud and Beyond, with Margaret Black. These books constitute not just excellent introductions to the work of particular schools within psychoanalysis but the ways in which the various ideas that are being discussed can be thought about in concert with one another without reducing their separate idioms or stripping them of their unique and particular contribution. In this way, Mitchell has consistently shown the connections - what he might call the relationality - between theories being thought about and developed at particular moments in history and the ways in which these are not necessarily oppositional accounts but differing ways of organizing what it is possible to see and understand. Not that he is inclined to fudge the differences which can be acute. His gift, in this area of his work, is to show both the commonality and the differences between tendencies, schools of thought, bodies of knowledge. He draws out the core of their connectedness while letting their differences stand in relief to one another.

Science, Metaphor and Meaning in The Interpretation of Dreams

Anne Samson MA PHD

Anne Samson

19 St Mary's Crescent, Leamington Spa, CV31 1JL

Anne Samson  

I

When I first read The Interpretation of Dreams something like 30 years ago I seized on it with excitement. It seemed to speak to me with great immediacy about my own internal processes. Returning to it recently as a student of psychoanalytic theory, I have been struck by its elusiveness, its resistance to any simple understanding. My first encounter with the book was, perhaps, something in the nature of an expeditionary raid from which, ignoring what seemed obscure or alien, I returned with the plunder that attracted me. My later encounter has been more like a settlement, an attempt to inhabit it and understand it in its own terms.

This enterprise is not easy, because inscribed in the texture of the book is an indecision about the very nature of psychoanalysis, an indecision that has become the subject of longstanding debate: is it a science or does it ally itself more easily with the humanities? Are the truths it seeks to establish historical or narrative? In the first part of this paper I shall show how this indecision appears in Freud's attitude to science, and leads to ambiguities in his notions of meaning and interpretation. I shall also argue that such ambiguities were probably historically inevitable, and have been fruitful to the subject. The second part of the paper will have a more practical emphasis and I will consider the usefulness of Freud's ideas of interpretation to the understanding of dreams of patients.

In his preface to the third English edition of The Interpretation of Dreams Freud wrote, ‘Insight such as this falls to one's lot but once in a lifetime’. That the insight was significant, and fertile for Freud as well as his readers, is indicated, not only by the number of editions of the book, but also by the way in which it retained its life for him. Of the 10 German editions eight are described in the Penguin edition as being enlarged and revised. The book, as we have it at the end of its career, is a palimpsest rather than a completely unified whole. However, somewhat paradoxically, the book remained rooted in his topographical model of the mind, and he made hardly any attempt to bring it into line with his later structural model. This somewhat ambiguous relation to time displayed in the history of the work after its publication - constantly emended, but rooted in a discarded mode of thought - resonates with the ambiguities this essay won the Prize for 1997.

A Tribute to Marion Milner

Nina Farhi

Nina Farhi

11 North Square, London NW11 7AB

Nina Farhi  

Some five years or so ago, in the midst of a solid, icy Saturday morning, I looked out of the window at the raging blizzard and realized that there would be no Squiggle seminar on original themes in the work of D.W. Winnicott that morning. No one could possibly brave the snowstorm and come.

Ten minutes before the seminar was due to start - the roads as hard white as the sky was dark, the house empty of all but my husband and myself - the door-bell rang and in walked Marion accompanied by a terrified taxi-driver clinging on to her. The driver, looking imploringly at me, told me how he had tried to dissuade her from her journey. Marion, however, sailed into the house quite unperturbed and apparently unaware of our astonished misgivings. The driver did not know, of course, that he had had a tiger as passenger!

I had the sublime good fortune to count Marion as a beloved friend for only 20 years. I am aware there are many others here who knew her well long before I was born.

I knew her - or felt I did - perhaps 10 years before meeting her when I first read her work, experiencing something that never really changed for me, even after coming to know her years later.

Here was a visionary whose lambent prose and visceral imagination distilled all that was dense, diffuse and seemingly beyond representation into a form that could be embraced with wonder, fear and deep excitement. You needed to read only one line to know that this was Marion Milner's work.

She was fired by an intellectual discipline and an artistic sensibility of such rare mettle that allowed her writing to rise, descend and intermingle in such conjunctions that it became infused with that pellucid fire which inhabits the work of the great mystics.

And yet what more fully embodied a being could there have been than her! Her distinctive elegance, her luminous beauty - vivid until the end - calls to mind her own words when writing about the inter-relation between what the eye saw and what flooded up from within - ‘a warmth and a glow and a delight’. This is how she looked at the world and this is the light she cast on it.

Back to Freud's Texts: Making Silent Documents Speak by Ilse Grubrich-Simitis. Published by Yale University Press, New Haven, CT, 1996; 322 pages; £25.00

Mark Solms

Mark Solms

London

Mark Solms  

This is a major work - the most important contribution to Freud scholarship since The Origins of Psychoanalysis was published in the early 1950s. The book is divided into three parts, the second of which is the main source of interest. The first part consists in an essay on the history of German-language editions of Freud. This is a comprehensive account, which reveals the complexity of internal and external factors that influenced not only the publication but sometimes also the content of Freud's works. One is struck by the amount of time and energy that Freud and his early followers devoted to the practical task of disseminating his ideas.

The second part of the book reports on preliminary research, conducted at the Freud Archive in Washington, in preparation for a proposed new German edition of Freud's collected writings. It has long been recognized that the existing German editions are - to say the least - ‘unsatisfactory’ (Strachey, in Standard Edition 1, p. xv). Grubrich-Simitis wants to establish the new edition on exacting historical-critical principles. She therefore considers the original handwritten manuscripts upon which the existing printed texts were based. Her description and analysis of these documents fill eight chapters.

The first of these chapters describes Freud's approach to the act of writing itself, based on a brief survey of his own comments in this regard. We learn that the widespread belief that writing came easily to Freud - that masterful lectures, articles and books simply flowed fully formed from his pen - is an idealization. Grubrich-Simitis describes the exacting internal and external conditions Freud required in order to be able to write. Of particular interest is her discussion of the depressive and maternal aspects of his creativity. However, she repeatedly emphasizes that it is not her intention to study Freud's personality. In an age when Freud scholarship increasingly threatens to degenerate into investigative journalism, her interest is focused firmly on the texts.

Daniel Miller

Daniel Miller

Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT

Daniel Miller  

The Non-Discipline of Material Culture Studies

In six days we are told God made the heavens and the earth and all the creatures therein, giving them their forms and their due. Rather more than a few days later, another set of creatures was created which we may call the academic disciplines. These creatures on further inspection look just as bizarre as any of those in the natural world, and their inspiration looks something rather less than divine.

Why are the things we learn and teach divided up into the categories we have come to expect? In my university (University College London) there is a discipline called geography where people who study rock formations are expected to have coffee with people who study urban ethnicity. An entire discipline of linguistics was given over to the study of language, another called psychology seems to mix and match expertise on emotional breakdowns with those who spend their time guillotining rats; while engineering has come to combine building bridges with building biotechnology.

I know of no grand myths for the creation of the modern disciplines (though there are classical precedents), but sometimes I imagine some moment of creation which I take to be reminiscent of a Kiplingesque just-so story. In it I see a thin young woman representing the world of artifacts - what we call material culture. For some mythical reason she seems to be arriving rather late at the crucial gathering. Upon arrival she discovers that all the other areas of possible enquiry are already leaving with their prized new disciplines from which they could create their identity, but, coming last, she finds to her horror that all the available disciplines have been given out and that nothing is left to her.

I imagine this abject waif expressing astonishment at her rejection and remonstrating with the great creator of disciplines:

How can such a thing be? Surely I should be the grandest of them all. Look who depends upon the study of artifacts. How can architects understand the effects of the buildings they create without a theory of the artifact, how can archaeologists who have to reconstruct ancient societies entirely through the uncovering of left behind artifacts work without material culture, what would guide designers in their work, who could study children playing with toys, what is it economists and business studies theorize about if it is not the demand for goods? How can we leave all these disciplines without even the consciousness that there is some wider field that unites them all and through which they can converse? That was my promised destiny.

Introduction

Over 20 years' practice in psychiatry and psychotherapy I have been impressed by the difficulties experienced by mental health staff in general (and psychotherapists in particular) when dealing with aggression in treatment relationships. As a young trainee I observed that colleagues who were competent in dealing with their own aggression handled aggression in patients more skilfully than those whose relationship with their own aggression was ambivalent, and speculated that aggressive competence was a necessary skill to be acquired in training. I was, however, struck by the almost complete absence of any mention of this aspect of therapeutic behaviour in textbooks, seminars or case discussions. A subsequent observation was that mental health staff and psychotherapists seemed uncomfortable to acknowledge their aggression, much less to use it. Discussion of overt or covert aggressive strategies in case management often provoked agitation and defensiveness, and led me to speculate that people with anxiety or ambivalence about their own aggression might select themselves for careers in mental health. A third observation was that patients, especially those who had been the subject of ill treatment or abuse, had a tendency to provoke re-enactment of that experience in treatment relationships, and that the process was often handled clumsily by the therapist with negative therapeutic consequences. Over the years, experience both as a practitioner and as a supervisor has reinforced these observations and led to the speculations that therapeutic aggression may be an important skill which psychotherapists are reluctant to use because of the personal dynamics which originally brought them into the profession.

Introduction

This case and two of the commentaries which follow were originally given at a conference held in June 1995 sponsored by the Chicago Center for Psychoanalysis in conjunction with the Chicago Association for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. Dr Michael Horowitz kindly agreed to write up his case and Drs Paula Fuqua and Frank Summers were able to produce written versions of the commentaries they had given extemporaneously at the meeting. Because of increased attention to different forms of psychoanalytic thinking among psychoanalysts and psychotherapists world-wide, the conference organizers thought it would be interesting and useful to hear one case followed by comments made by analysts who represented different schools of thought. A frequent conference format in our area consists of a case presentation, followed, firstly by formal discussion and, later, by informal discussion from the floor. Commentary from the Object Relations Point of View

Frank Summers

Frank Summers

Frank Summers  

The case of Mr L demonstrates the value of an object relations perspective on the psychoanalytic process. Dr Horowitz points out at the outset that what ‘stands out’ for him is conducting an analysis with ‘someone who deeply wanted to have one [an analysis] but almost as deeply could not bring himself to have one’. The question for the analyst is: why, given that he wanted an analysis to improve his career and severely restricted social life, did he have such difficulty ‘bringing himself to have one’? His initial analytic dream displayed his fear that the analyst was an ‘ugly hooker’ who would ‘tear his insides out’. Mr L could see even at this early point that beginning analysis led to feelings of ‘exposure, abuse, desire to make myself more shameful’. What will be exposed? The recounting of his history makes clear that he has borne a painful sense of inadequacy all his life. He suffered ridicule from the family members who raised him in addition to the excruciating shame of numerous episodes of waiting for his father who did not appear. He was humiliated for being a ‘sissy’ as well as for being male. Also important to Mr L's shame is the fact that the whole family is shame-prone. The parents treated their divorce as a defect that must be hidden. The charade that the parents were still married for years after their divorce reflects the inability of the family to accept the reality of their lives and display a realistic sense of themselves to others. Mr L lives in continual fear that his ‘defect’ will be exposed to others. Should they see how defective he is, their cruelty is akin to ‘tearing his innards’ out.

The anxiety of others seeing his defect is at the root of his paranoia. When Mr L says he is given to ‘nasty projections’, he is referring to his experience of others when he feels they ‘see inside’ him. When Mr L is not perfectly understood, he feels exposed, and this feeling of exposure accounts for the intensity of his reaction. Mr L's pained response to an imperfectly attuned analytic intervention forces him into awareness of his need for the analyst's understanding and the shame of this experience is unbearable. Under these conditions, he fears and sometimes believes that the analyst is in collusion with his mother ‘to plot his demise’. From his viewpoint, if the analyst did not have malevolent intentions toward him, he would not force him into such painful awareness. His family humiliated him for his needs, so if the analyst forces awareness of his needs upon him, he must be acting in concert with them. Consequently, he has no reason ‘to think everything you're saying isn't a calculated attempt to make me angry’. The more painful awareness that he cannot yet come to is the shame that underlies the anger.

This is a very long and expensive book, and it is worth every penny. Written by one man and therefore carrying its integrity from within that man's brain, it will not be superseded for a good many years - a good investment for researchers, scholars and teachers and fascinating background reading for clinicians, if we are content to browse rather than agonize over every single phrase. As a sample, here is a passage from Chapter five, the chapter that summarizes the arguments Schore is going to substantiate at length in the rest of the book. The italics are mine.

The central thesis of this book is that the early social environment, mediated by the primary caregiver, directly influences the evolution of structures in the brain that are responsible for the future socio-emotional development of the child. The resulting variety of dyadic affective interactions between the caregiver is imprinted into the child's nervous system… Different types of stimulation are embedded in these… interactions and they elicit distinctive psychobiological patterns in the child… In response to socio-environmental experiences, hormonal and neurohormonal responses are triggered, and these physiological alterations are registered within specific areas of the infant's brain which are undergoing a structural maturation. (p. 62)

…The mother's role as an external regulator of the child's internal affective state is essential in providing the child's limited nervous system with the modulated stimulation that optimally enhances the growth of (the infant's) affect-regulating structure… She directly influences the growth and assembly of brain structural systems… that perform self-regulatory functions (in the child)… This emergent adaptive function essentially mediates the individual's interpersonal and intrapersonal processes throughout the lifespan. (p. 63)

For once, I am willing to forgive the condensed and highly abstract style of writing, with its long meandering sentences. To have written this book in acceptable English would have made it four times as long, and to have shortened it would leave out important considerations. To make it easier, each chapter ends with a summary which we can consult to help us decide whether this is a chapter whose full text we need to read. Moreover, we are also helped throughout by the tactful arrangement of the material. The first 70 pages of the book summarize the latest views on brain structure and function, as well as the latest from multi-disciplinary studies (including psychoanalytically orientated ones) of infantile emotional development. With this as context, we arrive at Chapter five, the chapter which gives us an overview of the arguments we can pursue for the next 450 pages.
