Narrative is today's iconic word. Each of us has a narrative, a personal story. This emphasis on narrative may be a response to the collapse of wider collectives, the grander narratives of the twentieth century, Marxism, Communism and so forth. Narrative gives a sense of uniqueness, of being special: ‘l'état, c'est moi’.

This book sets out to locate the narrative component in selected well-known nineteenth and twentieth century English novels and to see how this interlinks with the therapeutic process. It makes for an interesting project. After all, both enterprises, writing and therapy, share similar perspectives - both are exploratory, to do with the unfolding of a drama, and both aim for some form of resolution. In the authors' own words, the books they have chosen aim to show

the engagement of the two [central] parties to change, the nature of the mutual influence they have upon one another; and the source of directionality in this influence, i.e. what makes the interaction a constructive one. (p. 34)

Here I have a difficulty. The quotation shows the rather dogged language used by the authors, often weighty and jargon-ridden, especially when lain alongside Jane Austen, say, whose prose style is liquid gold. Writers in our field need to lift their prose style to a more engaging and accessible plateau - otherwise our -isms may simply join the list of departing - isms mentioned above.

The first book studied is Pride and Prejudice - a welcome choice for British readers in view of the recent TV serialization, Elizabeth and Darcy now being part of most people's personal landscape. The authors set out their stall:

We will first review the events of the story, to acquaint and remind the reader of Pride and Prejudice, putting particular emphasis on personality, interaction and internal change. We will also refer to those aspects of psychoanalytic process that are suggested by the events of the novel, using standard analytic terms, but also introducing our schema of the therapeutic narrative for comparative purposes. (p. 24)

Although Holmes agrees that attachment is a new paradigm he implies that it is compatible with all existing psychoanalytic traditions. Bowlby would not have agreed with this as his writings make clear, so it is a new proposal. This, I would argue, is similar to New Labour in that many of the preceding government's principles are adopted in the New Labour paradigm.

In the first chapter Holmes develops his thesis summarized by a chart, Figure 1-1, where the psychoanalytic influences on Bowlby's attachment theory are shown as Klein, Balint and Winnicott. In fact, Bowlby's preferred object relations theorist was Fairbairn who is given little space until Chapter 4. This first chapter covers well the development of attachment theory and its breadth, but in my view he transforms it into an umbrella which can uncritically contain the divergence of psychoanalytic approaches.

The second chapter is a summary of the controversies around attachment theory and psychoanalysis where the idea of a conflict free umbrella theory is proposed. Holmes writes:

Klein places aggression and destructiveness much more centrally in her map of the human heart than does Bowlby, and so can perhaps more easily account for the intractability, resistance, and masochism that psychoanalysis so often reveals.

Klein, Bowlby, and Freud are not necessarily in conflict; they can be thought of as addressing different levels of psychological functioning.

Charles Rycroft  

When I first read the title of this book I expected and hoped that it would be an autobiography recounting the experiences, subjective and objective, that had made the author into a psychotherapist. But, in fact, it is a conflation of papers originally read to mental health professionals, especially psychotherapists, over an eight year span in Australia and New Zealand.

But nonetheless the book has an autobiographical flavour. As Anton Obholzer points out in his Foreword, Neville Symington's career has been characterized by social dislocation. It has taken him from the port wine trade into the Catholic Church, and then later to the Tavistock Clinic and the Institute of Psychoanalysis, and from Portugal via England to Australia. And The Making of a Psychotherapist does indeed record, although in a haphazard and disorganized fashion, the various impressions and opinions he has gathered and formed during his career as an analyst and psychotherapist, but without any explanation as to why he moved from the Catholic Church and Portugal to the psychoanalytical movement and London. As a result there is something tantalizing about the book: it arouses one's curiosity as to why the author left the Catholic Church and why later he left London for Australia, but fails to satisfy it.

In Britain Symington is accounted a member of the Independent Group of analysts and, as with so many members of this group, his attitude towards theory is idiosyncratic.

Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy Vol 11 No 3, 221-241, 1997

Working in a World of Bodies: Defensive Techniques on a Medical Ward -a Psychoanalytical Observation

Wilhelm Skogstad

This paper describes the observation of a medical ward carried out in a general hospital in weekly visits over a period of four months, and attempts a psychoanalytic understanding of the observations. Nurses working with physically ill patients face deep anxieties and conflicts, particularly fear of death and illness, of being overwhelmed by their feelings of pity, guilt and resentment; but also fear of the sexual impulses that close physical contact with patients stirs up. The paper shows that these anxieties were dealt with by a number of defensive techniques. Although the nurses sometimes showed the ability to be sensitive, the general culture was very defensive. The various defensive techniques commonly used are described and illustrated. Amongst them were: manic excitement and erotization; a constant moving of patients with little recognition of their feelings about that; a strong use of the body, so that patients were often not related to as whole persons; and defence mechanisms of a particularly concrete kind.



Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy Vol 11 No 3, 211-219, 1997

The Body of Thought: Psychoanalytic Considerations on the Mind-Body Relationship

Joan Schachter

This paper is an introductory review of a complex area of development and pathology. Psychoanalytic thinking about the mind-body relationship originated in Freud's studies of hysteria, in which the patient's body exhibited the unresolved mental conflicts. Subsequent psychoanalytic research into early development focused on the emergence of the psychological self from the early mother-infant relationship with its predominantly bodily experiences. The vicissitudes of the mind-body relationship have to be considered within the context of development of object-relationships and affect regulation.

Introductory Remarks

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

As many of you know, the Journal held lectures given by individuals for a number of years. Over the last three or four years we have been staging debates, because we feel that they create an encounter between different perspectives that can perhaps be particularly fruitful. From my perspective the fact that this lecture sold out some weeks ago speaks for itself, and we are absolutely delighted that you are all here.

Both our speakers are eminent in their own fields. Blake Morrison has been commentating, in both memoir and journalism, for some years, on childhood, masculinity, and the relationship between parents and children, most notably in his book about his father, And when did you last see your father? Anne Alvarez has more than 30 years experience of treating autistic, psychotic and borderline children and adolescents as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist.

The book which forms the occasion for this lecture, As If, evolved from a piece of reportage in the New Yorker. As many of you know, Blake Morrison writes about the trial in 1993 of children, Robert Thompson and Jon Venables, for the killing of 2-year-old James Bulger. As If is a book that has already been taken very seriously by workers in the law, social work and the probation service. It was in part because I was impressed that here was a book taken seriously by fellow professionals, and I could see the potential links with issues of concern to psychotherapists, that I proposed that we invite him to give this lecture and I was extremely pleased to have the enthusiastic support of my colleagues in the Journal.

Now Blake Morrison does much more than report a trial. He considers the way an event in the public domain permeates the mind; the way it revives memories of an earlier self, individual and collective; the questions it poses about being a child. We wanted the opportunity to hear the questions that he raises - which I think are centrally questions of meaning and memory - debated in our own field.

It may be less well known that Blake Morrison has been one of the judges of the Mind Book of the Year since 1991, and in 1996 Mind published a collection of writings on mental distress of which he was one of the co-editors. In the introduction to Mind Readings the editors remark on ‘how hard it can be to translate experience, the reality of the psyche, into language’. Two things struck me. One was a similarity, in that form of words, with what is struggled with in psychotherapy, and certainly what we struggle with in the British Journal of Psychotherapy. It is also true that the experience that As If depicts is a very hard one, that of witnessing a murder trial.

On Childhood and Violence

Blake Morrison

Blake Morrison

Granta Books, 2-3 Hanover Yard, Noel Road, London N1 1BE

Blake Morrison  

I suppose most people have an opinion on the subject of childhood and violence, but few people have an informed opinion. It is a bit intimidating standing here to realize that some of the people with informed opinions are probably in this room. I am not an expert and in many ways it feels a presumption to give this lecture. I think all I can do is to offer you my observations on what is, I suppose, the most notorious case of childhood violence in recent years, that of Robert Thompson and Jon Venables, whose month-long trial for murder in Preston, as Ann has said, I attended four years ago this month.

I want, in effect, to tell you a story. I'm encouraged in this by noticing how often, in books of psychotherapy - those few I have read - and indeed in the British Journal of Psychotherapy, a narrative of some kind (usually a case history) is used to illustrate some theoretical point. I hope to weave in my thoughts and conclusions as I go along, but there is just one thing I would like to emphasize at the beginning. The 1989 UN Convention on the Rights of the Child recognizes

the right of every child alleged as, accused of or recognized as having infringed the penal law to be treated in a manner consistent with the promotion of the child's sense of dignity and worth… and which takes into account the child's age and the desirability of promoting the child's reintegration and the child's assuming a constructive role in society.

Naively, perhaps, I went to that trial in Preston with some such underlying assumption of good will, imagining that all those professionally involved with the Bulger case - lawyers, social workers, teachers, police officers, journalists and psychiatrists - would want to elucidate the circumstances and the motives of that terrible crime, and would constantly have in mind the reintegration and the rehabilitation of the children involved. I was wrong. Few of them did. This was an adult murder trial, with the two ten-year-old boys at its centre viewed by all but a few there as practised and cunning adult criminals. Hence, I think, most of our thinking about this case has been badly skewed from the start.

Nina, Anatta and ‘No-Self’

Paul Williams

Paul Williams

Flat 1, 15 Rosslyn Hill, London NW3 5UJ

Paul Williams  

This short contribution to the memory of Nina Coltart is concerned with an aspect of the influence of Theravada Buddhism on her clinical work and, to some extent, her life, which has, in my view, certain implications for the work of psychoanalysts and psychotherapists which have remained largely unnoticed. This is the concept of anatta (‘no-self’). A history of the idea of anatta is beyond my capacity and the space here to provide, so a brief definition only is possible for the purpose of orientation towards its relevance for psychoanalysis. The linguistic term ‘self’ is translated in Pali as atta and in Sanskrit as atman. There are many related, conventional uses of the term atta (including to represent ‘conscience’), and these co-exist freely with the doctrine of anatta or ‘no-self’. It is at the level of psychological analysis and the Buddhist pursuit of ‘ultimate truth’ that atta is problematized, and it is this particular aspect which interested Nina. In a monograph on the relationship between psychoanalysis and religion, Nina cited the Buddha's Three Signs of Being (which are common to all peoples) in order to draw attention to the apparent contradiction between anatta and our use in the West of the terms ‘self’ or ‘ego’ (Coltart 1993). The Buddha taught firstly that all beings suffer ‘whether crudely or subtly, whether on a small or a grand scale’ (Coltart 1993); secondly, that all human experiences, including thoughts and feelings, are transient and impermanent; and thirdly, that there is no Self. To the Western mind attuned to a Christian, socio-political and psychological emphasis on the primacy of the individual, not to mention the orientation of the practising psychoanalyst or psychotherapist, this is a startling and rather difficult notion. In her usual constructive and insightful way, Nina disentangles the paradox by referring to the quality of illusion and transformation common to both Buddhist and psychoanalytical discourses. In mutative psychoanalytical and authentic religious experiences there occurs a similar sense of awe as profound, object-seeking impulses are mobilized in the service of ‘the unthought known’, to borrow Christopher Bollas's term (Bollas 1987). Obviously the two transformational experiences are different in a great many respects but they both share a destabilizing outlook towards the self and the other. For analysis to be successful, the psychoanalytic patient must suffer the slow, skilful disillusion of the transference as it wends its way compellingly towards resolution. In Theravada Buddhist practice the realization that the existence of a discrete, personal self is an illusion is a core tenet of the teaching. Akihisa Kondo (1983) has described the role of illusion in suffering in Buddhism and psychoanalytic psychotherapy, taking examples from Horney's work. One might add that the two disciplines are concerned more with what the self is not, rather than what it is.

Michael DelMonte

Michael DelMonte

Dublin

Michael DelMonte  

This is a special book indeed. One goes on hearing with monotonous regularity that Freud's theories are essentially untestable, and thus have not been scientifically appraised, and on the few occasions that this has been attempted little, if anything, was forthcoming in Freud's favour. Given this context, it is somewhat surprising that this book has not received more publicity - especially in psychoanalytic circles. This may have to do with the discomfort that many psychoanalysts feel when confronted with the Anglo-American logical positivist approach inherent in this book, with its emphasis on quantification and controlled experimentation. However, it can and has been argued that positivist and relativist positions are both valid but different methods of inquiry into human nature - albeit at opposite ends of the investigative continuum (DelMonte 1997). In this light this book offers a complementary scientific approach to answer the accusation that Freudian theory is nothing but wild, unbridled and unscientific speculation. One can see this book as a direct challenge to those psychoanalysts like Donald Meltzer (1978) who repudiate any need for psychoanalysis to come to terms with ‘scientificity’.

This publication is confined solely to Freud's theorizing. It does not address the huge corpus of neo or post-Freudian perspectives developed over the past century. Fisher and Greenberg, in their introduction, contrast the scientific empirical approach with the hermeneutic stance taken by many, if not most, psychoanalysts. They are both clinical psychologists who, throughout the text, remain faithful to the perceived merits of the empirical approach, whilst attempting to portray Freudian thought in its full complexity. This is not always easy.

In all, Fisher and Greenberg review a formidable 2500 research studies. This is achieved by expanding on their previous publication in 1977, in which approximately 1800 studies were reviewed. They were critical of faulty and dubious research designs, and highlighted those studies with ingenious and apt approaches to testing Freud's theories - for example, those utilizing subliminal messages presented tachistoscopically in conjunction with projective response instruments such as the Rorschach and the Thematic Apperception Tests, among others.

Editorial

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

It could be claimed that, as the clinical practice of psychoanalysis has developed during this century, there are three concepts that have exercised some of the best minds and altered the way in which psychoanalysis is thought about and practised - the concepts of projective identification, narcissism and the countertransference. It could also be said that though these three concepts are of quite central concern today, they are embedded in competing models of the mind. Put very simply, these models could be described as the ‘intrapsychic’ versus the ‘interpsychic’. John Gedo (1973, p. 10) suggested that ‘Models of the mind are summarizing conventions which represent the clinical theory of psychoanalysis’. This notion of models of the mind being ‘summarizing conventions’ is a useful idea to bear in mind as we see both the ‘interpsychic’ and ‘intrapsychic’ being used in this issue. The concept of projective identification is essentially an intrapsychic phenomenon and Duncan Cartwright argues for two components to it: the affective component and the self/object component, which need to be distinguished if effective therapy is to take place. Robert Royston approaches the problem of narcissism through the lens of the interpsychic and examines the consequences of the failure of the object to reflect positive and self-affirming experiences in the infant. This can leave the infant with an internalized ‘anti-self object’ composed of its own ungratified narcissistic needs as well as the narcissistic needs of the caretakers. The ‘anti-self object’ becomes a most destructive carapace against change. Patricia Marsden and Gillian Russell locate their work with bulimic patients in the intense intrapsychic countertransference that such patients invoke in their therapist. They distinguish three countertransference feelings that this particular pathology can arouse in the therapist: a feeling of failure, a feeling that they have become cold and hateful, and finally a feeling that the therapist needs help. It is perhaps at this intense edge of borderline despair that the concept of the Working Alliance is most needed. However, this concept is a bit ‘slippery’, as Jane Kitto points out, not least because there are competing theories of mind upon which this concept rests.

Jane Kitto

Jane Kitto

2 The Park, London N6 4EU

Jane Kitto  

This paper was stimulated by the recent paper by Charlotte Wynn Parry and Diana Birkett (1996) in which the authors suggest that the idea of the working alliance has dropped out of analytic discourse and they suggest that it be brought back. In this paper I suggest that, rather than having dropped out, the idea of the working alliance has some inherent difficulties and also that it arises in relation to a particular view of the mind and mental functioning and correspondingly of the nature of the therapeutic process. Since we do not always distinguish clearly enough between these different models there is room for confusion. This paper does not aim to resolve confusion but to make some suggestions about why some of the confusions arise in the first place.

Processes of Love and Separation in Jane Austen's Mature Work

Bernardine Bishop

Bernardine Bishop

7 Patshull Road, London NW5 2JX

Bernardine Bishop  

This paper considers Jane Austen's later novels in terms of a process towards emotional maturity. It conceives this specifically as the maturation of the capacity to love, and of the development of that capacity from narcissistic undifferentiation to true relatedness. The degree to which the object of love is seen as separate from and other to the self is seen as crucial in this evolution.

[[RunningHead]]

Charles Rycroft

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes  

With the death of Dr Charles Rycroft at the age of 84, British psychoanalysis has lost both one of its most lucid exponents and its severest critics.

Rycroft was born in 1914 into what he liked to describe as the ‘lower upper classes’. His father was a fox-hunting baronet, who died when Charles was 11, leaving his mother depressed and relatively impoverished. The young Rycroft was sent to Wellington, where he joined a group of ‘type B Wellingtonians’, which included the poet Gavin Ewart, a lifelong friend. Although destined for an army career, he chose instead Cambridge where his intellectual gifts and left-wing sympathies were soon apparent. He briefly joined the Communist party, and, influenced by Virginia Woolf's brother Adrian Steven, became interested in what was at that time the subversive discipline of psychoanalysis.

After a year as a history research student, he applied for analytic training, but, by his own account, was considered by Ernest Jones, the doyen of the British psychoanalytic society, to be a dilettante, and so was asked to qualify in medicine first. His medical training was at University College Hospital, and later he worked briefly in psychiatry at the Maudsley Hospital, before setting up in private practice as an analyst in 1948, continuing to see patients until a few days before his death.

His first analyst was Ella Sharpe, who may have stimulated his interested in metaphor. After her premature death he was treated by Sylvia Payne (he used to joke about the ‘sharps’ and ‘pains’ of analytic training), and rose quickly in the British Psycho-Analytical Society, becoming assistant editor of the International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Scientific Secretary, and a training analyst, with R.D. Laing perhaps his best-known analysand. Towards the end of the 1950s however, he became dismayed by the rivalry between the Kleinian and Freudian factions, and began to question the scientific credentials of psychoanalysis. He quietly withdrew from the psychoanalytic society, devoting instead his considerable literary talents to a wider audience. Throughout the 1960s and 1970s he reviewed prolifically for the Observer, New Society, New York Review of Books, and the New Statesman, evaluating the major figures in contemporary psychoanalysis and psychology. He produced several highly influential books including A Critical Dictionary of Psychoanalysis which has been continuously in print since it appeared in 1968, and The Innocence of Dreams (1979), which he considered to be his finest work.

David Stafford

Margaret Fagan

Margaret Fagan

Margaret Fagan  

We at the Arbours Crisis Centre are sad to announce the death of our colleague David Stafford (1957-1997). David is remembered by all of us for his kindness, helpfulness and clinical ability in working with people in severe states of emotional distress. He is also remembered for the generous and lively support he offered to his colleagues. David began his career in mental health work with the Richmond Fellowship and came to the Arbours Crisis Centre as a resident therapist in 1979. This is an unusual and demanding job requiring personal stamina and solidity as well as technical expertise. The resident therapist lives at the Centre and is available to the residents to offer help and support at a time of breakdown and crisis. Residents at the Centre could readily recognize David's ability to contain immense distress and challenging behaviour, without becoming overwhelmed, ‘bogged-down’ or retaliatory. Whilst at the Centre, David met Suzanne, a social work student on placement, who was to become his wife.

Subsequently, David qualified as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist with the Association of Arbours Psychotherapists and also graduated in psychology from Brunel University. For the next few years David developed his expertise as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and began his work with the families and children of alcoholic parents. He became Director of the St Joseph's Centre for the treatment of addiction (part of Holy Cross Hospital, Haslemere) and set up the Co-Dependency Clinic there. Concurrently, David was a founding member of the National Association for Children of Alcoholics, and became its chairman in 1996. This was the position he continued to hold until his death. David's book Children of Alcoholics (1992) was based on his insights from this work and was reprinted in 1996. David's first book, An Agreed Understanding (1987), discussed parent and professional communication in the light of the 1981 Education Act, and Co-Dependency (1991), written with Liz Hodgkinson, concentrates on the treatment of addiction to drugs and alcohol. David also worked in private practice.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon  

That there is such a thing as a history of psychoanalysis in Russia might seem surprising given that there was no psychoanalysis to speak of there for 60 odd years. Etkind's book, first published in Russian in 1993, is a fascinating, if rather idiosyncratic account of a relatively brief period of psychoanalytic endeavour and it is a tribute to the author's imagination and scholarship that he has written such an extensive book on such little material.

The flourishing of psychoanalysis in Russia was brief, lasting from about 1910 until the early 1930s, and yet it prompted Freud himself to speak in 1912 of ‘a local epidemic of psychoanalysis’ (p. 3). There was, it seems, more interest there than in France or even Germany at the same time.

Three key figures stand out - Lou Andreas-Salome, Max Eitingon who later headed the International Psychoanalytic Association, and Sabina Spielrein, Jung's first analytic patient (and lover), who returned to her native Russia in 1923 and would be murdered by the occupying Germans in Rostov. The impact of psychoanalysis on Russian culture was immense. The Symbolists, including the novelist Andrei Bely, were greatly influenced by it. The great polymathic thinker, Mikhail Bakhtin, was engaged in a dialogue with psychoanalysis throughout his life, and it was probably he who wrote, under another name, what remains to this day one of the most important critical engagements with Freud's thought, Freudianism: A Critical Sketch, usually attributed to Volosinov. The film-maker Sergei Einsenstein not only sought psychoanalytic treatment but was profoundly influenced by its ideas. So too was there an enormously fruitful engagement with psychoanalysis by the central figures of the influential Soviet psychology such as Lev Vygotsky and A.R. Luria.

Despite Lenin's dismissal of it as a fad, psychoanalysis flourished particularly in the astonishingly creative years after the 1917 revolution. Nearly all Freud's works were translated into Russian and achieved significant sales - the two-volume Introductory Lectures sold 2,000 copies in 1922 - and there were, of course, serious attempts to achieve a synthesis of Freudianism and Marxism, a project supported not only by people such as Luria and Vygotsky, but also by leading Bolsheviks such as Trotsky and Radek. There was in Moscow an unprecedented State Psychoanalytic Institute and the Psychoanalytic Orphanage, a specialized establishment for the children of high-ranking functionaries, who included Stalin's son. By 1923 the 30 members of the Russian Psychoanalytic Society comprised one-eighth of the total membership of the International Psychoanalytic Association.

Francesca Raphael

London

Francesca Raphael  

Despite the rave reviews on its back cover, and positively sycophantic foreword, I found this a self-important and disappointing book. The author takes ‘Poiesis… the creative act, the death and rebirth of the soul’ as a focus. His aim in the book is ‘to question the meaning of suffering’ and to explore ‘how, in the face of human fragmentation, art making can find its therapeutic power’. These are huge questions. In his attempt to answer them, the author hauls us through philosophy, anthropology, mythology and many other disciplines. There is a richness of material here indisputably, but I was left with the uneasy feeling that breadth is no substitute for depth and that rhetoric was masquerading as profundity.

Each of the nine papers that make up the book was in fact written for nine different occasions and different audiences, which gives an uneven and fragmented feel to the book. We meet Freud, Shamanism, Descartes, Apollo, Nietzsche, Jung, Winnicott, Klein - I could go on and on - in a fairground ride of ideas that left me with an impression of riches, but dizzy. The style of writing is a mixture of philosophical discussion, self-assertion and rhetoric, with little or no reference to clinical material; the sole exception to this is an example from the author's own therapy to which I will come later. This makes for a very ungrounded text in which the reader is expected to go along with his almost religious fervour despite the paucity of evidence to support his views.

He holds some strong views. Take, for example, ‘The task of therapy is not to eliminate suffering but to give voice to it’ (p. 15), or ‘Art provides the container in which pain can be borne, without this container the psyche cannot hold its suffering’ (p. 57), or, similarly, ‘Art has an inherent capacity to heal the psyche…’ (p. 2) - well, maybe it has, maybe it hasn't, let's have some examples to consider, to grapple with.

His statements are generalizations; is he talking about all patients, psychotic and neurotic alike? Children and adults? Is expressive arts therapy a panacea for all ills? Here we come to a key weakness with the book; the reader is not invited to think for him or herself, but to believe, agree and applaud. The book's central premise, namely that art and psychotherapy are ‘essentially united’ (p. 6), is left entirely unsupported and unargued. I felt he was preaching to the converted which made me want to argue with him throughout.

John Clare

John Clare

John Clare  

The central thesis of this book is that psychoanalysis, as an idea, is socially constructed but then becomes interwoven into the taken-for-granted meanings of everyday life, especially our notion of the self. The approach will be unfamiliar to some in that it presents a sociological perspective; Parker is concerned not specifically with clinical practice but rather with psychoanalysis as a theory in the world and of the world.

Using discourse analysis, Parker goes playfully back and forth between how culture gets into psychoanalysis and how analysis permeates the culture. Psychoanalysis can explain ideology but is itself an ideology. Freud's theories are rooted in the Enlightenment and the economic and cultural features of the nineteenth century and yet they have influenced the development of their antithesis in postmodern. fragmentation. Drawing on Foucauldian approaches to discourse, Parker teases out the interweaving of psychoanalysis and culture to capture the Freudian nature of subjectivity. He reminds us that this reflexive capacity is relatively recent, bringing to mind Foucault's observation that perhaps all but a minority of people could have reached the depressive position in medieval society.

Locating psychoanalysis as part of the modernist project, he is sceptical about its role as the master key to open up culture, a metanarrative with which to finally explain the world. Contrasted with this absolutist view is the postmodernist stance of Lyotard, Lacan and Zizek in which the omniscience of psychoanalysis, socialism and other grand narratives has given way to so many little stories with perpetual speculation on the impossibility of truth. Editorial

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles  

‘Is psychodynamic psychotherapy only suitable for the middle-class elite?’ ask Guthrie, Moorey, Barker, Margison and McGrath in their paper on ‘Brief Psychodynamic-Interpersonal Therapy’. In most NHS psychotherapy departments and in voluntary organizations dealing with the deprived in inner city centres it is appalling to witness the cruelty and abuse that man inflicts on those he is close to and depends upon. Can psychotherapy alleviate this suffering? Can it bring about lasting change? And perhaps, the question that is most often asked today, can psychotherapy give some account of itself? These authors describe ‘a conversational model’ of brief eight-session therapy that concentrates on the ‘here and now’ of the relationship between therapist and patient. The sample is with three extremely damaged women for whom all other types of therapy have proved unsuccessful. The six-month followup questionnaire suggests that they all benefited from this encounter.

Perhaps the most persuasive way in which psychotherapy is, at present, giving an account of itself is in the work of attachment theory. Attachment theory has the possibility of a research methodology built into it. In Samuel Stein's paper, ‘Enuresis, Early Attachment and Intimacy’, he argues that attachment theory is well documented and that it is a good description of human development. He then takes a case of secondary enuresis in a 10-year-old boy and shows that a change in the maternal attachment of this young boy brought about a relief in his symptom.

The theme of the ‘intrapsychic’ versus the ‘interpsychic’ which was a theme in the last issue (BJP 15(1)) is spelt out in great detail by Stephen Mitchell in one of the papers given at the Fifth Annual John Bowlby Memorial Lectures. Stephen Mitchell in ‘Attachment Theory and the Psychoanalytic Tradition: Reflections on Human Relationality’ addresses the early conflict between the ‘attachment tradition’ and the ‘psychoanalytic tradition’, and the way in which we are witnessing a rapprochement between these two ways of thinking about ‘mental events’. He argues that Freud never lost sight of the view that ‘the clinical process of psychoanalysis has always been fundamentally relational’. However, during the interwar years, the ‘intrapsychic’ experience was emphasized at the expense of the ‘interpsychic’; the analyst was seen as the scientific observer of the mind of the patient and the intersubjectivity of the analytic experience was left unexplored. Mitchell links the overemphasis of drive theory, or the ‘intrapsychic’, to the culturally dominant Cartesian belief that the only true knowledge we have is of our own minds. It is the work of Bowlby, Stack Sullivan, Fairbairn, Winnicott and Loewald, Mitchell suggests, that has most powerfully challenged the (‘artesian hegemony of drive theory’. Mitchell's account of the conflict between attachment theory and drive theory argues for a clear view that each theory is incomplete without the other.

The Antigroup: Destructive Forces in the Group and Their Creative Potential by Morris Nitsun. Published by Routledge, London, 1996; 318 pages; £16.99

Jessica Johnson

Jessica Johnson

London

Jessica Johnson  

The ‘antigroup’ is a concept that Morris Nitsun has developed for describing and understanding the negative disruptive, destructive elements that threaten the functioning of the group. It evolved out of his extensive experience as a group analyst and has already had a major impact on the theory and practice of group psychotherapy. Here he extends it also to non-clinical group contexts including organizations, staff groups, experiential training groups, the family and our culture at large. Interplay between creative and destructive tendencies is central to the group analytic process, and a theme which he develops beautifully is the transformational potential of antigroup tendencies and their contribution to aesthetic depth.

In more ‘pathological’ situations, though, the psychotherapy group can feel gripped by countertherapeutic processes that are insidious and hard to understand or seem to have come out of the blue, for example, sudden negative therapeutic reactions, spiralling destructiveness or prolonged negativistic impasse. Bion's description of ‘group mentality’ evokes images of the group as a morass of ‘anonymous contributions’, primitive impulses estranged from their original sources through projective identification. As Morris Nitsun shows, this reflects the complexity of the group process but also the need for coherent, clinically based conceptual frameworks for guiding the group therapist in this challenging area.

This book develops such a framework. It shows that it is possible and important to identify and understand these destructive processes more clearly. Through extensive clinical illustrations Morris Nitsun shows how this can enhance the group therapist's capacity for containing, limiting, integrating and harnessing the creative potential of otherwise inexplicable group destructive forces. This is timely as group therapists work increasingly with borderline and psychotic patients and in settings such as the NHS where disturbance and destructive processes in the host organization can resonate in the consulting room.

M. Davids

M. Davids

London

M. Davids  

Psychoanalytic therapies reach a disproportionately small number of poor patients and ones from minority ethnic and cultural backgrounds. This leads to a widespread perception that in the West psychoanalysis - like much of the establishment - has a systematic, if unconscious, bias against members of such groups. Rose-Marie Pérez Foster, one of the editors of this volume, puts it succinctly:

As psychoanalytically trained clinicians, we carry a secret shame. While being members of a field that prizes the value of all human life, and people's efforts to realize their fullest potentials, analysts also know that they, in fact, touch a very narrow range of people… Our hidden shame is that psychoanalysis has a very defined view of life and how it should be lived, and it is this perspective that determines who is to be treated, who is analyzable, who has adequate ego strength, who can meaningfully relate to objects, and who is capable of exploring his or her deep inner self… The bold fact is that we work best with those people who are most like us, the middle class and educated who basically think and live the way we do. (p. 3)

This important and timely book tries to address directly the widespread view that, contrary to its claim to have found ways to access universal mental phenomena, psychoanalytic theory and clinical technique in fact do not apply seamlessly across the boundaries of culture and class.

The Psychoanalytic Mystic by Michael Eigen. Published by Free Association Books, London and New York, 1998; 220 pages; £15.95

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

London

Josephine Klein  

I was attracted to this book by its title, and there are interesting pages in it: a summary of Freud - oceanic feeling and the (also pre-oedipal) father as a centre of psychic drama; long and frequent musings on Bion and Lacan, both of whom Eigen admires - O and jouissance; and useful clinical material including some vignettes. But I was disappointed for several reasons.

Firstly, I have the impression that he has not read other writers - mystical or psychoanalytic - in a scholarly way. I am no enthusiast for Bion or Lacan, and no scholar of theirs either but, when Eigen rhapsodizes about (ostensibly) Bion's O, I do not recognize it as faithful to Bion's intentions. Eigen quite allowably is less concerned with ‘ideas about’ mysticism than about what he considers to be mystical experiences; he is experientially based. But Bion's O has, I think, something to do with ultimate meaning or deepest significance, and is focused and worthy of focus. Similarly, it is my impression that Lacan's jouissance is more precise and austere than Eigen's version of it. Readers will need to judge for themselves.

Secondly, Eigen appears to define as mystical all or most experiences of depersonalization or loss of personal integration, and only these. He, and the people he works with as a soi-disant analyst, experience waves of sensation, often unpleasantly, and to these Eigen attributes mystical status. Indeed he writes as though he equates them with jouissance and/or O. He values these states highly, and sometimes attributes to them something of the status given to the encounters which Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had with their God. Eigen is very much not of the quietist persuasion. The encounters seem uproarious, rumbustious, like Handel's setting of ‘For He is like a refiner's fire’ and, as far as I can judge, without moral content. If there is an encounter, it is with something that has nothing of interest to say. The medium is the message. It is like attributing deep significance to a roller-coaster ride, and Balint (1959) has already done this very well.

Rosine Perelberg

Rosine Perelberg

London

Rosine Perelberg  

In his 1915 paper on the Unconscious, Freud already put forward his thesis that the unconscious is present in the gaps between the observable. The psychoanalytic domain is the domain of that which is, in fact, not accessible to observation but can only be reached through its derivatives. Thus it is easier to say what it is not than what it is: an absence of negation, of a sense of time, characterized by thing presentation, symbolism and metaphors. The psychoanalytic domain is thus characterised by that which escapes us all the time, and which makes its presence felt through its absence. The capacity to bear uncertainty and not knowing may become especially difficult in situations which are traumatic like in child sexual abuse.

These thoughts were evoked in me by reading Ann Scott's courageous and lucid book, which tackles central issues in contemporary psychoanalysis. The author takes the reader on a journey through many scenes: from Freud's clinical cases to theatre and literature, from the therapeutic setting to ads in newspapers, from a scrutiny of the psychoanalytic literature to the observation of sugar packets in a café near London's Oxford Circus. One can only admire the fluidity with which the author moves between these domains, establishing links, inviting reflection and expressing her capacity to sustain psychoanalytic thinking. Central to the book are the connections between memories, phantasies, events and reminiscences and how these relate to a conceptualization of time. Organizing all these conceptual concerns is the issue of sexual abuse and what psychoanalysis has to offer to its understanding.

The first chapter reproduces a paper Ann Scott first published in Feminist Review in 1988. Already at the time I thought it was one of the clearest contributions to the feminist discussion about the way psychoanalysis had failed to make a clear contribution to the issue of sexual abuse. Whilst acknowledging Freud's failure in realizing the external reality of sexual abuse, Ann Scott pointed out the importance of what had been discovered after the abandonment of the seduction theory.

The Clinical Thinking of Wilfred Bion by Joan and Neville Symington. Published by Routledge, London, 1996; 198 pages; £14.99

Alan Lidmila

Alan Lidmila

Alan Lidmila  

The work of the eminent psychoanalyst, Wilfred Bion, is best described as being particularly concerned with the notion of thought as a bridge between truth and fiction, sanity and madness. As the Symingtons say, Bion's ideas are therefore to do with imprisonment (constriction) and freedom. Much so-called thinking, often positioning around bubbles of ideas that masquerade as solid substances, locates self and others either inside the compound or Bion the pale. Ho! Ho! What might have interested Bion is not whether such a joke was a good or bad one but whether, in true psychoanalytic fashion, it was interesting and also helped develop thinking further. Reading this book certainly helped develop my thoughts about Bion because it refreshed the parts that original readings didn't always reach. Clearly the Symingtons have enjoyed writing in a similar way as I have enjoyed reading. If this much-needed volume enhances, as Barthes would say, our pleasure of the text, then the writings of Bion can't be that difficult. Now, be honest, there can't be many sentiments you've come across in black and white that have associated Bion with intellectual knockabout fun and pleasure. But hist, something sober this way comes; Ha! ‘Tis the cloak of seriousness, a must for all true clinicians’.

How did the Symingtons achieve this impressive effect of seriousness and good humour around a project that is, after all, an exegesis of sacred texts? Mainly by warning us that Bion's ideas are complicated and that the book will ‘not absolve the reader from hard thinking’ (p. xii), and then going on to make complex ideas accessible, especially through the judicious use of interesting examples in myth and resonant ones in clinical experience.

The organization of the book is clear and straightforward enough - which is something to be appreciated given its subject matter. A helpful introductory chapter discusses the relation of Bion's thinking to Freud and Klein, and makes the point that Bion was neither a Freudian nor a Kleinian and was very much his own man even to the extent of causing some Kleinians to dissociate themselves from some of his more metaphysical thinking.

Critical Review of the Review of Psychotherapy Services in England

David Taylor

This review of the Review has become something of an historical paper. It addresses the context and climate in which the Review's recommendations were originally formulated. The government has changed since the review was published in September 1996. With it, there have been some alterations in the political context which have rendered the points made a little, but only a little, less immediately with us. However, the potential of the human psyche to generate and to respond to the type of superego mental-functioning I try to describe remains, even if there are a few signs of lessening severity. For this reason, the points made retain some long-term relevance. Last but not least, the momentum established by the Psychotherapy Review offered a real opportunity for progress and development.



Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy12(2), 103, 1998

Reflections on Purchasing Psychotherapy Services: The Importance of Unconscious Factors

Antony Garelick

The ambivalence towards psychotherapy services, underlying oedipal anxieties and the sense of exclusion from the therapeutic dyad, is explored. Their significance and the role of unconscious factors and their interplay with organizational dynamics are discussed, drawing on personal experience. Their importance in the purchasing of psychotherapy services is considered and the development of helpful strategies is described.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis79, 27, 1998

Disavowal of Reality as an Act of Filial Piety

Bernard Penot

The author argues that often the hidden power of disavowal of reality gradually makes itself felt in a treatment. The psychoanalytic process then seems to have been brought to a halt by something that defies meaning and continually eludes any genuine subjectivization by the patient. In the famous case of the Wolf Man (1918) Freud speaks of a rejection of reality, which he clearly distinguishes from repression, in that the rejected representation has not in any way been erased from consciousness; rather, its meaning remains as if in suspension, no longer open to judgement. Certain key moments in the treatment of a borderline case help to illustrate the necessity for the analyst to grasp the peculiar nature of his own involvement. He may have been induced to assume a parental attitude reproducing a ‘community of disavowal’ that belongs to the patient's unrecognized history. By adopting an interpretive formulation acknowledging his own participation in the disavowal - which the parents must have been unable to do - the analyst can then allow the patient to get out from under it. These considerations allow us to shed light on two possible theoretical difficulties regarding, firstly, the difference between negation and disavowal of reality and, secondly, the way that the disavowal tends to hamper the very process of symbolization necessary for the deployment of fantasy.

Elizabeth Mehlman  

The psychological development of non-borderline adult patients raised presumably by mothers with borderline characteristics is examined. Despite childhoods that were subjected to a preponderance of pathological interactions with a primary caretaker, the adults described exhibit common patterns of adaptation that have enabled them to achieve higher levels of integration and differentiation than their mothers. Characteristics of adaptation include self-understanding, sublimation, the ability to form positive relationships with other caretakers, and the constructive use of fantasy. In treatment, these patients present a number of issues such as fluctuating self-esteem, anxious attachment, a ‘borderline transference’, and a conflicted identification with the mother.

The Work of Transformation: The Seduction of the Broken Object

Tessa Adams PHD

Tessa Adams

New Cross, London SE14 6NW

Tessa Adams  

There have been various accounts as to the nature of primary satisfaction that the fragmented object can provide for us. We can look to Peter Fuller's psychodynamic interpretation of the Venus de Milo as one notable example. The statue, he tells us, transcends its mutilation by offering us a site for our maternal projections - its random breakages touching upon primary repression. His view is that the Venus is more seductive than her intact counterparts since, with pitted surface and absent arms, we meet the body at once ideal and broken, signifying the mother who has survived our infantile attacks. That is to say, Fuller sees the Venus' damage as paradoxically enhancing on the basis that it is a statue which can offer us a representation of the ‘whole object’ in Kleinian terms. He maintains that, in embracing its mutilation by aestheticizing its flaws, we meet again our earliest bid for reparation.1

It is from this perspective that I will consider the work of Cornelia Parker, a contemporary British artist, who purposefully challenges the boundaries of the object. I will focus on two of her most striking installations: Thirty Pieces of Silver (see Figure 1) and Cold Dark Matter: An Exploded View (see Figure 3) and interpret the impetus for each work. This discussion will be set within the context of other art works which feature artistic preoccupation with destructive/reparative processes. Here I refer to Rachel Whiteread's famous House (see Figure 5), that concrete interior which met its public demolition against a background of considerable controversy, and to the images of damage in death that Damien Hirst so blatantly exploits through his formaldehyde edifices. This exploration will be framed by Kleinian principles and look towards assessing these artists' intentions as to their transformative ambition.

It is recognized that Melanie Klein's theory of child development differs from Freud's in her focus on the infant's pre-oedipal struggle for autonomy. This is a task which demands the transition from primitive, part-object cathexis, termed the paranoid/schizoid position, to the capacity for full-object relationship by the end of the toddler years. This struggle, termed the depressive position, is seen to be resolved through the infant's acceptance of the mother as a ‘whole object’. Which means that the infant's early perception of a world of part-objects (in which good can only be split from bad) is seen to give way to the realization that ‘good’ and ‘bad’ exist as aspects of the ‘whole’.2

Enuresis, Early Attachment and Intimacy

Samuel Stein

Samuel Stein

Samuel Stein  

Enuresis is a common childhood problem which, although it causes considerable distress to both children and parents, nearly always responds to at least one of the available treatment modalities. These treatment options include behavioural techniques, cognitive therapy, medication and psychotherapeutic interventions. However, both behavioural treatment and pharmacotherapy have high relapse rates. In spite of the general acknowledgement that enuresis (especially secondary enuresis) indicates underlying psychological problems, few cases are described in the literature where a psychodynamic approach was used successfully. This is especially noticeable given the growing acceptance that enuresis is related to sub-optimal parenting, poor child-rearing practices and disruption of maternal care. The clinical vignette described is a case of secondary enuresis in a 10-year-old boy which responded favourably to psychodynamic input after behavioural, cognitive and family therapies failed to resolve the problem. The dynamic formulation postulated a desire for intimacy, following failed mother-infant bonding due to maternal depression, which was obtained through enuretic symptoms and interpersonal conflict. This quest for intimacy through replication of early pleasurable somatic sensations and the utilization of conflict for attention-seeking may rapidly develop into a repetitive cycle involving delinquency, crime and sexual perversions later in life. In such cases, a psychodynamic understanding is most likely to succeed as the enuresis represents an ego-syntonic solution to possible ego-fragmentation, or an attempt at preventing pending psychological breakdown.

A Tribute to Marion Milner

Michael Podro

Michael Podro

1 Provost Rd, London, NW3 4ST

Michael Podro  

Marion had drawn and painted as long as she could remember and she described herself as a Sunday painter. (But she took her painting seriously enough to go and work for several periods with Cedric Morris who was a very distinguished teacher, of Lucian Freud among others.) As everything she did was caught up in everything else - because she was constantly placing her different activities in the context of each other, seeing how they could illuminate each other, painting couldn't remain a separate, self-contained enterprise; she recruited it, famously, to her self-reflection, with characteristic courage asking why she found her painting so unsatisfying and what that might betoken.

For instance, she wrote on the use of colour:

I noticed that a smear of paint on the left of the palette after painting, where white merged into red, blue, brown, was interesting and alive; whereas the picture painted with the same colours but carefully separated was dead.

She then observed that matching the colour of her green paint and the green of the object to be painted produced ‘a terribly dead effect’. What was at issue was not only the effect of fortuitous merging as opposed to the controlled separation or matching of pigments - a basic issue for anyone who falls in love with the medium of painting - but how this could be a matter of what was alive and what wasn't - and why the taught techniques of painting seemed to stifle vitality. (Her thought in this passage on paint is expressed in a way that seems to relate it back to infancy, to her account of the infant's disillusion that its gift of faeces ‘is not as lively, as beautiful, as boundless as the lovely feelings they had in giving of them’. It is the true artist, in love with his medium, who can overcome the disillusion and give life to it.)

Perhaps the problem of the medium of painting became, for her, unresolvable - something that could be released only episodically from the puritan constraints of taught technique. Whether this was so or not, her sense of the inner life that animated painting became identified with its imagery; and because of this her concern became not so much with producing pictures as responding to the images that emerged - and the skill she developed was that of letting them emerge, of not foreclosing on them: she would then wonder what they could mean, what stories they prompted her to tell.

Commentary by a Kleinian Psychotherapist

Meira Likierman

Meira Likierman

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 6BA

Meira Likierman  

Many details in this full and vivid account deserve attention, and a commentary will necessarily be selective. My choice is to approach the task with a focus on two different points in the material which particularly draw my attention: one is the patient's highly revealing ‘Christmas turkey’ dream, and the other is the technique adopted by the therapist, especially as evident in the difficult session described at the end.

First the dream. In the initial part of it the patient, B, is trying to get rid of two old carpets, both of them reminding her of ‘trampled and well-worn’ carpets which actually existed in her childhood home. In the second half of the dream, B finds a cooked turkey which has been left over from Christmas. This turns out to be still fresh under its foil wrapping and its skin. In the session B is able to provide associations to the dream and some valuable analytic work follows.

I would go along with the therapist's conviction that the old carpets represent B's parents. The patient has every reason to think of both of them as having led downtrodden, ‘trampled’ lives and as having been worn down by their difficulties. More specifically, her mother was continually down-trodden by her father, while he himself was worn down by his repeated, and ultimately fatal psychiatric illness. Unlike the therapist, though, I feel that the carpets are not simply ‘the parents’ but, more specifically, their worn-out, depressed and now destroyed aspect. B's desire in the dream to rid herself of the two carpets is thus not a straightforward rejection of her parents. Rather, it suggests her struggle to be rid of an underlay of depression left in her by her exposure, since childhood, to her parents' unhappiness. B knows that both her parents not only died prematurely, but died after leading considerably unhappy lives.

The Lacanian Subject: Between Language and Jouissance by Bruce Fink. Published by Princeton University Press, Princeton, New Jersey, 1995; 219 pages; £13.50.

Many years ago I visited Chambord, a well-known château on the Loire. One of its chief claims to fame is a spectacular double spiral staircase. If you climb one set of stairs, then intriguingly (and also rather disturbingly) you can see people climbing the other at the same time. My irrational and illogical expectation was that at some point my path would cross with that of the people ascending the other staircase but, of course, only at the top on the balcony did I meet them!

There is a need for a view from the balcony. As with other forms of psychoanalysis, in a Lacanian analysis the use of speech is the main tool, the whole treatment may take a number of years, the analysand may be invited to use the couch and some relief of a human being's suffering may occur as a result. Therefore, like the staircases, the starting and endpoints are not in precisely the same place, but nevertheless bear some relationship to each other since the architecture of the enterprise is essentially the same.

Bruce Fink's A Clinical Introduction to Lacanian Psychoanalysis is the first book I have come across in English which sets out in straightforward terms, the clinical approach adopted by Lacanians and links it in an accessible way to some elements of Lacan's extremely complex set of theories. Fink assumes no previous knowledge on the part of the reader and he has a beautifully clear style. I tested the accessibility factor by asking a number of non-Lacanian practitioners to read it as well as consulting the views of Lacanian friends. Unlike many books it seems to have been welcomed across the range of opinion in the field. After all, it is easy to warm to a book which invests an old joke (how many psychoanalysts does it take to change a light bulb?) with a new set of meanings. He illustrates how a Lacanian analyst works with the patient (or analysand) with examples from his own clinical practice and those of his supervisees.

Love: Paradox of Self and Other

Hester Solomon

Hester Solomon

Flat C, 262 Finchley Road, London NW3 7AA

Hester Solomon  

Unlike fictional literature, analytic literature contains relatively little about love. Of course, there are exceptions,1 but by and large, analytical attention has addressed other, often negative, emotional states much more consistently and systematically. Perhaps it is truer to say that it has given them a higher profile, as if they were, for the clinician, more pressing, more interesting, more exciting or perhaps more easily thought about. Attention to hatred, envy, jealousy, perverse and violent feelings, anxieties, depressions and psychotic states and various forms of attacks on and retreats from the possibility of psychological transformation, has ensured that much of our analytic thinking remains focused on negative states of mind. And yet, states of loving are nothing less than the driving emotive force underpinning much of the physical development of the self and propelling much of the self's psychological development from birth until death. Love is certainly one of the primary emotions at the core of object relating, and this has deep implications for the impact of love on the relationship between patient and therapist. However, the fairly copious use of the term ‘erotic’ (for example, the ‘erotic transference’, and the far less frequently described ‘erotic countertransference’) is often a signal that the state, attitude, or feeling being designated is considered to be pathological. Hence, we see little in the analytic literature about the love that a patient might feel for their therapist, or the therapist for their patient, or indeed about the love that might be shared between them.

It would be tempting to broach an object relations account of love by making a series of theoretically accessible and easily identifiable distinctions: between erotic and passionate love on the one hand and agapaic and compassionate love on the other; between love experienced and expressed from within the paranoid/schizoid position or from within the depressive position; between the evocation of the rule of abstinence which forbids any form of abuse of the patient and an equally professional stance which may seek to formulate interventions, however carefully fashioned, designed to penetrate or at least soften the most hardened defences as a. necessary prelude to change; or again, between the analytically familiar notions of idealization and denigration and their apparent correlates in loving and hatred; and, not least, between forms of love and forms of hate.

While we sit and take this in, I am not sure I should be saying anything at all. A moment's silence or something probably seems more appropriate. Anyway, thank you very much. I couldn't see how you were going to select from your book because it is such a vast subject, and such a painful one.

I just wanted to start with your last reading about the whole issue of forgiveness. I have to say I am not a forensic expert, I am not a forensic psychiatrist or psychologist. I am a clinician who thinks about these issues, really only as a clinician, so I am sure there are people in the audience who have things to say that possibly are more relevant than I have. But I wanted to think a little bit about John Major's statement that we must condemn a little more and understand a little less, because it reminded me very much of a very interesting paper by Neville Symington that was in the International Review of Psycho-Analysis, I think in the late seventies. He was talking about responses evoked in analysts by working with the psychopathic patient. I think these responses are aroused in us when we hear about a psychopathic crime, even if the murderers weren't actually full psychopaths, or psychopaths at all, and were in fact just small children. These responses that he identifies are: condemnation, collusion and denial. And he thinks that these are perfectly appropriate reactions but they are very unhelpful in the treatment, and that the analyst has to work on his countertransference responses to transform these into very different responses which have something to do with really having the courage to look evil in the eye - which doesn't mean that the perpetrator himself is necessarily evil.

I think what I want to say is that there isn't any short cut to this forgiveness that we are talking about, either in the abused, in the abuser, or in the witness, or maybe even in the nation; and that some of the outrage and shock and dreadfully superficial condemnation - that you are so against and that has stimulated you to write this very important book - is also appropriate. It may be unprocessed, but I don't think there is a short cut in any of us, really, to the forgiveness. It is very interesting that you make that very passionate speech about it at the end of your book, and you tell us what you went through in the writing of the book and the sitting through the trial.

The Value of Revenge in Analytic Theory and Practice

Paula Collens BA

Paula Collens

UCL, 3 Taviton Street, London WC1H 0BT

Paula Collens  

The Value of Revenge

Vengefulness (is)… part of human potential and a common aspect of interpersonal connectedness

(Feiner 1995)

In developing a discourse on the subject of revenge, it is useful to begin by asking what value such a discussion holds for the field of analytic theory and enquiry, and how this subject is relevant to psychotherapeutic practice.

The quote above offers a succinct answer to the first of the questions raised - revenge, as Feiner suggests, is an integral aspect of human capacity and of relationship and therefore germane to analytic discussion. Surprisingly, however, a review of the analytic literature reveals that there is a dearth of focused dialogue on the subject of revenge. In fact no substantial core text directly or exclusively addressing this theme can be located; however, fertile ground for thought and application can be found in papers relating to the subject. This limited exchange on the subject of revenge is highlighted by Socarides, who asserts that ‘Vengeance - one of the most persistent and powerful emotions of man - has had little attention from scientific investigators’ (1966, p. 157) and Feiner (1995) infers that social embarrassment about such emotions contributes to the way in which revenge has been ignored. Indeed he suggests that ‘we do seem to feel more content when we assume its appearance is attributed to the more disturbed. Nevertheless, our vengefulness, like our shadow, is there’ (1995, p. 381).

Taking up on the second point raised: how is the concept of revenge pertinent to psychotherapeutic practice? Since revenge is an aspect of human potential and interrelatedness, this potential may be mobilized in either the client or the therapist within the therapeutic alliance. Racker's (1974) attention to the talionic nature of the transferential relationship, and Jacobs's (1995) assertion that ‘Revenge is one of the reasons why we are in the caring business’, embody two of the main reasons why a discussion of this concept is relevant to therapeutic practice.

Combative and provocative, this is a book that stimulates or infuriates according to the readers' relationship to the conditions Showalter diagnoses, or to the groups she criticizes. It has been widely reviewed, so rather than attempting to encompass the large canvas it covers, I shall focus on the book's reception and its delineation of Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS) as a psychogenic epidemic. As someone who since 1984 has worked with patients presenting with CFS, my concern is whether hysteria is a useful or even accurate diagnosis.

There are three sections; histories, cultures and epidemics. As a literary historian as well as a historian of psychiatry, Showalter has a great deal to offer in the first two sections which cover the history of the concept of hysteria, an examination of narrative representations of hysteria in the context of gender difference, and a critical analysis of feminist interpretations of hysteria. However, Showalter is not simply presenting a cultural/historical analysis. This is a polemical text. ‘I believe our human dignity demands that we face the truth’ (p. 207), she declares, which begs the question, ‘Whose truth?’ Confident assertions of ‘the one truth’ sit uneasily in a book concerned with unconscious processes, and readers' and reviewers' protests have not been slow in coming. The book has had a turbulent reception, primarily from those groups who object to the classification of their physical illness as psychogenic.

Since the mid-nineteenth century, millions of people have migrated to Latin America, choosing to endure multiple losses in the anticipation that life in the ‘New World’ would offer a positive alternative to the limited opportunities in their countries of origin. Chilean poet Gabriela Mistral captures the complex but essentially optimistic essence of this kind of migration:

I am two. One looks back,

Attachment Theory and the Psychoanalytic Tradition: Reflections on Human Relationality

Stephen Mitchell

Stephen Mitchell

251 W. 71st St, New York, NY 10023

Stephen Mitchell  

I very much appreciate the invitation to present this year's John Bowlby Memorial Lecture. I have always found Bowlby's work stimulating and very important; he directly concerned himself with what has seemed central to me both in terms of theory and clinical practice. I met him once in the 1980s, when I served as a discussant of a paper on attachment and detachment he presented at the William Alanson White Institute, and have vivid memories of the stories he told about the British Psychoanalytical Society in the 1930s and 1940s, the early years of his intellectual maturity. I remember him commenting that ‘the pressures against looking at real life experiences were something ferocious’. In the discussion I wrote at that time, I noted that:

At a time when psychoanalytic theory often seems to be growing more and more jargonized and arcane, Dr Bowlby's work has been an inspiration for those hoping to see psychoanalytic theorizing remain open to other intellectual disciplines and informed by advances in research and clinical observation.

I would like to take this occasion to reflect on the relationship between the flourishing attachment tradition Bowlby's work established and the psychoanalytic tradition. I want to show how Bowlby's virtual expulsion from mainstream psychoanalysis in the early 1960s makes some sense in terms of the history of psychoanalytic ideas, since he was several steps ahead of his own time. I then want to consider the ways in which other major psychoanalytic authors, Fairbairn and Loewald, as well as the American psychiatrist Harry Stack Sullivan, struggled with the same problems Bowlby was dealing with. There is now a very marked receptivity among psychoanalysts to the same ideas that earned Bowlby his place in the psychoanalytic Gulag along with Fairbairn and Sullivan. Finally, I want to consider the way in which an integration of these different angles on the same phenomena car, be helpful both conceptually and clinically.

Psychoanalysis, has always been centrally concerned with human relatedness. The domain of psychopathology - psychoneurosis - that Freud wrested from the neurology of his day was a realm in which mental events, rather than the purely physical, had become problematic, and the mental events Freud concerned himself with from early on had largely to do with relations with other people.

David Mayers  

Dr Horowitz's style of case presentation is not a familiar one to me: I am used to far more sessional material, and proportionately less summary. My comments are, therefore, provisional and should be read as questions that I should like to put to him.

A general uncertainty relates to the title, and to his calling this ‘a successful analysis’. I don't have enough of a sense of what the criteria of success are, and of what is meant by an analytic space's being socially constructed. Is what the analyst considers primarily important the patient's being able to re-enter medical school and survive the first year there; and does ‘social construction’ refer to the patient's growing adaptive capacities as seen in the transference? It is not clear whether the analyst is highlighting this limited part of the transference to illustrate a thesis about the importance of the social, and passing over other important material as contextually irrelevant; or whether he does not value as I do the concerns that I am looking for and not finding. These can be grouped under three inter-related headings: the infantile, the sexual, emotional linking.

The Infantile

When the patient is first introduced he appears as a potentially abused child - he brings the evidence quite concretely in newspaper articles. Thus we learn of a broken family, the traumatic discovery of his grandmother's suicide on his bed, the heartrending picture of the children waiting for the father who doesn't turn up. But how are such things experienced in the work? What, symbolically, is the New York Times? How is the patient's lying on the couch to be unpacked in terms of the denigrating grandmother who kills herself and about whom the patient feels guilty - what does guilt mean here? The absent father is embodied in both the silent analyst and the silent or absent patient; but what is he doing in his absence, who is he with, why doesn't he want to be with his son? When the analyst, in the two brief clinical vignettes, refers to his relationship with the patient it always feels like one adult talking to another. I think that I would have wanted to introduce phrases like ‘from a little boy's point of view…’, and in general I feel that I don't have nearly enough sense of how the analyst experiences his patient's infantile phantasy life.

Abe Brafman

London

Abe Brafman  

Joyce McDougall's books have made themselves required reading in the psychoanalytic world. She has written extensively about sexual perversions and psychosomatic illnesses, both being problems that are not often part of every analyst's clinical experience. McDougall has original views on these subjects, as well as on the vicissitudes of the creative process, another issue in which she takes great interest. Because her hypotheses on the etiology of problems in these various areas take her to the earliest stages of infancy, McDougall has managed to interweave these formulations with theories on the development of the self, of the body self and their functioning both in health and when this breaks down.

Joyce McDougall writes with great lucidity and authority. Her ideas are based on rich clinical experience and she has an impressive grasp of the theoretical formulations of analysts from many schools of thought. When the typical analytic paper will quote exclusively from members of the author's adopted school, Joyce McDougall is conversant with and quotes extensively from Kleinian authors and from ego psychologists, Lacan and other French authors, Winnicott, and many others. However, Joyce McDougall follows her precepts and demonstrates that learning should be a step towards creativity and originality, and not part of a process of intellectual enslavement. The Many Faces of Eros is dedicated to her eminent friend, Robert Stoller, who devoted immense efforts to the psychoanalytic understanding of sexual phenomena and who first investigated in detail the link between the child's gender problems and the mother's psychopathology.

The Many Faces of Eros concentrates on the ‘psychoanalytic exploration of human sexuality’, but time and again themes and patients from her previous books are focused on in the discussion. In Theatres of the Body (1989) she studied the puzzle of psychosomatic illnesses and in Theatres of the Mind (1985) she addressed ‘illusion and truth on the psychoanalytic stage’. But already in her earlier Plea for a Measure of Abnormality (1978) we can find what proves to be something of a ‘leitmotiv’ for the subsequent books: the challenging argument that we must not belittle the difficulty of defining the dividing line between normal and abnormal behaviour, between normal/ healthy and abnormal/ pathological. Indeed, this problem is seen most clearly in the area of sexuality, where we tend to describe as ‘perverse’ or ‘abnormal’ most departures from vaginal penetrative heterosexual practice. McDougall argues that such views usually result from moralistic prejudice and she believes that we should accept these other sexual practices as forms of ‘neosexuality’, thereby emphasizing what she considers the creative aspect of those sexual activities which are, by definition, uncommon. She sees these various sexual practices as the individual's attempt to deal with intolerable psychic conflict throughout the course of his development, perhaps not so different from what is usually called ‘compromise formation’.
