Ken Wright

Ken Wright

London

Ken Wright  

Art therapy is a relatively new profession and is still in process of defining where it stands in relation to psychiatry, psychoanalysis and other psychotherapies. Having started life as a relatively submissive handmaiden of medicine - doing a bit of art in occupational therapy - it has gradually found its own identity, and is now well established as a form of therapy in its own right. If growing up involved separation and individuation, self-definition and a growing self-confidence in who one is, then art therapy may well claim to have made this passage rather successfully.

Katherine Killick and Joy Schaverien's book can be seen as a contribution to this process. In its twelve chapters, each by a different practitioner, different aspects of the profession are brought into focus. Anyone with the patience to read the book through 411 be rewarded by a rich and engaging perspective on this young profession.

The first six chapters are rooted in current practice and each is richly illustrated with clinical material. The aim is to give a picture of what art psychotherapists actually do and why they do it. Each writer elaborates a theoretical perspective - some more original than others - and situates the clinical story within this. Through this we get a number of different insights into the ways art psychotherapists relate to their patients, and how they think about them as their therapies unfold.

The second six chapters are more historical in perspective and attempt to understand the emergence of art psychotherapy, as a therapy rather than a pastime, within the large, and now vanishing, psychiatric institutions. At least three of these papers are autobiographical: that on ‘Art, Madness and Anti-Psychiatry’ by John Henzell, which gives an interesting insight into the more subversive strands of art therapy which could align themselves with Laing and other ‘anti-psychiatrists’; Claire Skailes's paper ‘The Forgotten People’, a moving account of her brave, and often lonely, attempt to establish art therapy within a traditional, institutionalized setting; and another moving and sensitive account by Sue Morter of trying to bridge the move into the community as a large institution closed. This is discussed through the impact it had on work with one highly deprived and disturbed individual.

Thomas Szasz

Thomas Szasz

4739 Limberlost Lane, Manlius, NY 13104, USA. E-mail: tszasz@aol.com

Thomas Szasz  

I use the term ‘psychotherapy’ as the name of a freely contracted relationship between two competent and responsible adults, one paying the other for assisting him, by means of a dialogue, to live his life better. In addition, I distinguish sharply between voluntary psychotherapy, whose wellspring is the patient's need for helping the Self and involuntary interventions called ‘psychotherapy’, whose wellspring is the family's (or the court's) need for controlling the Other. The former rests on consent, the latter on coercion. It is just as absurd to conflate voluntary and involuntary ‘psychotherapeutic’ relations as it is to conflate sexual relations between consenting adults and sexual assault called ‘rape’.

Psychotherapy for Ethnic Minorities: Issues, Context and Practice

Dinesh Bhugra and Kamaldeep Bhui

Kamaldeep Bhui

London SE5 8AF

Kamaldeep Bhui  

Psychotherapy is an effective tool in the treatment of many psychiatric conditions. Most psychotherapies were developed in the West and their application to minority ethnic groups is fraught with difficulties. In this paper we highlight some of the key issues that play a role in the therapist-patient interactions in different types of psycho therapies. The role of culture, race and ethnicity in relation to such an interaction is discussed. The main components of processes of psychotherapies are described and the role of training and research emphasized.

A Tribute to Dr Nina Coltart

Jan Abram

Jan Abram

18 Ridge Road, London N8 9LG

Jan Abram  

To behave as if - even worse, to believe that - we can treat anyone and anything with a hope of providing real help is to be caught into omnipotence, and the idealization both of psychoanalysis and of ourselves.

(Coltart 1993, p. 46)

Nina Coltart's work exemplifies the very best aspects of psychoanalysis - poetry and integrity, honesty and intuition, knowledge and uncertainty, silence and conversation. As a personality she created a deep impression on all who came into contact with her. The loss of her unique presence is still acute, but the rare quality of Dr Coltart's contribution will live on.

My perspective starts from the early 1980s when I, like scores of other psychotherapy trainees, benefited enormously from Nina's encouragement. If you sent a letter (she was a great letter writer) it was usual to receive a reply by return of post. She would gladly comment on essays, advise on career moves, refer patients, write references for many of us setting out. Nina typified the kind of great aunt any young woman embarking on a difficult career could wish for - warm, sanguine and incredibly facilitating. At the same time she was never sentimental, and her warmth was measured and containing. Although she was friendly, our relationship remained professional. I will always be grateful to Nina for her humanity, dedication and sense of humour. It was a great honour to have known her.

I have a vivid memory of the first time I saw Nina, perhaps mostly because it was the very first analytic lecture that I had ever attended. All of us study the person on the stage in a very particular way - after all we are allowed, even encouraged to stare. And a person sitting quietly by a table and looking slightly down created a striking picture. This was my first sight of Dr Coltart. As people entered the cold and lofty hall where the talk was to take place, every now and then someone would greet her and she would look up, smile (that incredible warm smile which made her eyes sparkle), nod, say a few words and then go back into her sort of self-reverie. She had whitish hair, was conventionally dressed, and I was aware of a heaviness about her shoulders - I had an unthought sense of her being weighed down by a heavy burden. Now I know something of Nina's tragedy, I can reflect that I may have sensed this at first sight.

Katherine Arnold

Katherine Arnold

Katherine Arnold  

The original material for this clinical commentary is from work with a patient with an eating disorder. I am very grateful to our anonymous contributor for very full and thought-provoking material, as well as the generosity and trust involved in sharing the difficulties of psychotherapeutic work with a wider audience through publication. The commentaries are as usual chosen to give an idea of work from different orientations, this time from two therapists working at the Women's Therapy Centre (which, of course, has a considerable reputation for work in this field, each therapist coming from different original trainings), from a Jungian analyst, and a Kleinian child and adult psychotherapist.

The themes of femininity and masculinity, and difficulties in being able to take in good experience within a relationship naturally emerge in all the commentaries, as does the commonality of being able to devote sufficient time to the exploration of the patient's thoughts, which is one of the hall-marks of psychoanalytic work. However it is possible to see the different emphases placed by the therapists, and to see how the diameter of the container, or the distance between patient and therapist, seems to vary according to the concepts which come most readily to mind.

B, a 26-year-old postgraduate student training to work with children with learning difficulties, has been attending therapy twice weekly for two years. B started to be bulimic when she was 16 following the traumatic deaths of her parents and grandmother within four months of one another. At the time of coming to therapy, she was faced with the task of clearing out the effects of the house she had inherited from her parents, and was also anxious that her boyfriend would ‘invade’ her space when he returned from his trip abroad. Another precipitating factor was the suicide of her first boyfriend earlier that year. She had attended his funeral, and cried for the first time since the deaths of her mother, father and grandmother.

My first impression was of a tall slim young woman with a classically beautiful face, in heavy boots, jeans and a large baggy jumper, tramping into the therapy room from her walk across the park. She sat down, embarrassed and awkward, like a shy and likeable adolescent. However, there was also a responsible, grown-up aspect to her, intelligent and with a sense that she had integrated some wholesome values somewhere along the line. In the countertransference I was aware of both a maternal desire to reach out to her neediness (scarcely hidden behind her veneer of pseudo ‘cool’ independence)

Ten members of the staff of the Women's Therapy Centre in London have contributed to the book entitled Psychotherapy with Women: Feminist Perspectives. It is a welcome contribution to the vast literature concerning the analysis of women which has arisen in the past few years. In this volume the contributors concentrate on the problems that may arise between the two women engaged in the therapeutic process, the analyst and the patient. Both women share the same gender identity and equally experience the same problems of separation and individuation from their own mothers who, in their turn, may have experienced the same problems with their own mothers. So that therapy may often become a three-generation process. The numerous problems that may arise in the course of therapy are discussed, such as problems of race in contemporary society, problems of women's relationships to their own bodies and those of their mothers.

Lennox Thomas  

This is a most interesting book in which the author presents some new ideas about the use of psychoanalysis particularly with those from ethnic minorities, and others on the margins of this mode of psychological treatment. Altman writes with conviction about the use of psychoanalytic therapy with low income groups and those who live on inner city estates. His writing is based on his experience of living in a split world, having a

273

practice in fashionable Manhattan with mainly white, wealthy patients and working in a state-supported clinic in the Bronx with largely African-American and Hispanic patients. Far from being confused by this he has been able to use his situation to appraise thinking on contemporary psychoanalysis.

I found the book stimulating and moving. The case histories are very alive and present him as a therapist with great warmth and sensitivity even in the face of the many constraints on analytic work in the US public sector. These were not the only difficulties because the Mandarins in the private sector did not seem to take the other part of his work seriously. From his tactful writing of this, one gets the impression that he was seen as idealistic and, maybe, a little misguided. Altman felt that the one part of his work informed the other. The book, he said, was written after he left his job in the Bronx.

In the United Kingdom the line between public and private psychoanalytic therapy does not ever seem to have been so clearly marked. The founding of the Tavistock Clinic in the 1920s played an important role for the development of good public access psychotherapy. The existence of a National Health Service in the UK made it more possible for mental health professionals from a variety of disciplines to train and to make their contribution in the public sector. That said, we need to be aware of the trends that have been set in the USA. Case management, cost effectiveness, simplistic efficacy research and Health Insurance funded treatment have dogged psychoanalytic therapy in the United States and are set to do the same on this side of the Atlantic.
